docs.text: Veylrath Clans ¶ The Veylrath Clans are the dominant peoples of the north-eastern half of the Veylrain Expanse, a vast rainforest region of canopy settlements, river routes, ancient ruins, and dangerous wildlands. They are often described as the more honourable counterpart to the Zul’Akari Clans : still territorial, still dangerous to outsiders, but far less cruel and far more willing to trade, guide, and negotiate. The Veylrath are not a unified kingdom. They are a clan-based rainforest society bound by shared laws, river agreements, sacred groves, ruin taboos, and mutual defence against monsters, invaders, and reckless relic-hunters. Ithrava ¶ Among the Tabaxi and many older peoples of the continent, Arkhaven is also called Ithrava , meaning "The Land That Breathes" . The name is older than the human arrival of the Ark and remains especially common in the Veylrain Expanse, where rainforests, rivers, ruins, and living canopy shape almost every part of daily life. To the Veylrath, Ithrava is not a poetic name. It is a way of understanding the land itself. The jungle breathes through mist, rot, blossom, floodwater, animal movement, and the slow return of roots over old stone. Government ¶ The Veylrath Clans are governed by the Canopy Concord , a council of recognised clan elders, river-speakers, pride leaders, huntmasters, shamans, and ruin-wardens. Each major clan controls its own settlements, hunting grounds, river crossings, and protected ruins. The Canopy Concord settles disputes between clans, regulates trade routes, punishes attacks on protected settlements, and decides when the clans act together against outside threats. Leadership is based on age, proven wisdom, family reputation, survival skill, spiritual authority, and service to the rainforest. Clan leaders are expected to protect their people, preserve safe passage through the jungle, and respect the old places beneath the trees. Dominant Peoples ¶ The dominant people of the Veylrath Clans are Tabaxi. Their settlements, trade families, hunters, storytellers, scouts, and relic-seekers define much of the region’s culture. The Veylrath also include lizardfolk, tortles, grung, firbolgs, kenku, shifters, hadozee, aarakocra, and small numbers of humans, half-elves, and gnomes living under clan protection or trade agreement. Tabaxi in the Veylrath Clans use one-word personal names. Family identity is shown through inherited body markings rather than surnames. Each family is born with distinct shared markings, and when two family lines merge, the markings of their children change into a new combined pattern. These markings are used to identify ancestry, kinship, inheritance, marriage ties, and clan belonging. Region and Biome ¶ The Veylrath Clans rule the northern-eastern half of the Veylrain Expanse. The region is dense rainforest, defined by humid air, heavy canopy, sprawling rivers, hanging moss, ancient trees, flooded roots, hidden ravines, and ruins swallowed by jungle growth. Many settlements are built high among the trees. Canopy villages use rope bridges, suspended platforms, carved walkways, woven lifts, and watch-posts hidden among branches. River settlements sit along major waterways and serve as trade stops, ferry points, fishing centres, and meeting grounds between clans. A settlement that seems small by human city standards may still be large, influential, and difficult to manage by Veylrath standards, especially if it controls safe river access or recognised canopy routes. The rainforest borders savannah and open country in places, allowing hunters, traders, and scouts to move between jungle trails, riverways, and grassland edges. These borderlands are important for monster tracking, seasonal trade, and contact with neighbouring peoples. Culture ¶ Veylrath culture is clan-based, practical, oral, and strongly tied to movement through the rainforest. The people value family markings, river knowledge, hunting skill, storytelling, relic lore, survival training, and respect for the old ruins. Trade is important. Families and clans maintain known routes between settlements, river crossings, savannah edges, and safe canopy paths. Reliable traders, navigators, and negotiators hold high status because they keep isolated settlements connected. Storytelling is central to Veylrath life. Tabaxi storytellers preserve family histories, warnings about dangerous ruins, accounts of monsters, trade-route knowledge, and tales of those who vanished by ignoring old laws. Children are taught through stories, but the stories are treated as memory and instruction rather than entertainment alone. The Veylrath do not forbid curiosity, but they place strict limits around sacred places. Ruins are studied, guarded, and respected. Looting ruins without permission is a serious crime. Relics are appraised by trained historians, shamans, and ruin-wardens before being moved, traded, or sealed away. Quiet Carriers ¶ The Veylrath distinguish between criminal smuggling and quiet carrying . Quiet carriers are clan-recognised couriers, river runners, and canopy messengers allowed to move goods, letters, medicines, warnings, and sometimes people without announcing their business to every settlement, foreign trader, patrol, or rival family along the route. This work is legal only while it serves clan law. A quiet carrier may hide cargo from outsiders, hostile powers, toll-takers, or reckless merchants, but not from the Canopy Concord, the relevant clan elders, or ruin-wardens when relics, cursed objects, medicines, or protected goods are involved. A quiet carrier who conceals a dangerous relic from the proper wardens is no longer a courier. They are a thief. Religion and Magic ¶ The Veylrath Clans worship many gods and spirits connected to the jungle, rivers, ancestors, hunting, family, moonlight, protection, and hidden knowledge. Each people keeps its own rites, but the rainforest itself is treated as a living inheritance shared by all clans. Shamans, spirit-speakers, ruin-wardens, and oral historians hold respected positions. Their work includes blessing trade routes, interpreting signs, protecting burial trees, identifying cursed relics, and teaching the laws surrounding ancient sites. Magic is present and respected. Veylrath magic is used for healing, tracking, concealment, animal speech, weather signs, river travel, warding, climbing, ruin study, and protection against monsters. It is less formal than the magic of elven courts and less academic than the magic of the Leridian Concord , but it is deeply adapted to rainforest survival. The Silent Canopy ¶ The Silent Canopy is a known region of deep rainforest within the Veylrain Expanse. Stories of it are common among hunters, traders, elders, and travelling storytellers. Common accounts state that wildlife avoids the area, the canopy blocks out nearly all light, ancient ruins within it appear in different places over time, and sound behaves strangely beneath the trees. Hunters and travellers speak of golden-eyed figures moving silently through the foliage, glowing markings carved into old stone, and statues appearing where no statues stood before. Older Tabaxi storytellers preserve the warning: “The jungle remembers what was buried there. It does not want it found again.” The Veylrath Clans treat the Silent Canopy as a forbidden and sacred danger. Travel into it is restricted by clan law. Relics taken from its borders are brought to ruin-wardens, historians, and shamans for judgement. Ancient Ruins and Relics ¶ The Veylrain Expanse contains many ancient ruins buried beneath roots, moss, strangler trees, and flooded stonework. Some ruins are used as shrine-sites, some are sealed, and some are watched by designated families or ruin-wardens. Relic appraisers and historians are respected figures among the Veylrath. Their duty is to identify objects, record their origin, judge their danger, and decide whether they can be kept, traded, studied, returned, or destroyed. The clans distinguish between discovery and theft. A relic found with permission and brought before the proper wardens brings honour. A relic stolen from a protected ruin brings punishment. Outsiders are not forbidden from studying Veylrath ruins, but they must do so through recognised hosts, scholar agreements, or clan protection. Kelshara is one of the few places where human scholars can work openly under these customs. The strictest rules are enforced at sealed ruins, sacred groves, burial trees, the Silent Canopy, and sites where the Canopy Concord has placed ruin-wardens. Tensions ¶ The main internal tension is between curiosity and caution. Young hunters, scouts, and relic-seekers are drawn to the old ruins, while elders and wardens enforce strict limits to prevent ancient dangers from being disturbed. The second tension is between isolated settlements and major trade families. Canopy villages depend on river routes and trade agreements, but powerful trading families gain influence by controlling maps, ferry points, safe trails, and access to foreign goods. The third tension is monster pressure. The Veylrain Expanse contains dangerous beasts, jungle predators, river monsters, venomous swarms, and ancient things that move through ruined places. Monster trackers are essential to clan survival.

docs.text: Windmere Assembly ¶ The Windmere Assembly is a wealthy, multi-racial state on the eastern cape of Arkhaven , built from human, dwarven, gnomish, halfling, and elven settlements. It is a fertile coastal assembly-state where rich grasslands, southern forests, mountain-fed rivers, and sea access have created one of the more prosperous societies on the continent. The Assembly is defined by shared government, productive land, racial cooperation, and commercial wealth. Its people are richer than most northern populations because the soil is better, the climate is kinder, and landowners with good farmland hold significant economic power. Government ¶ The Windmere Assembly is governed by an elected representative body known as the Grand Assembly of Windmere . Each major people of the state sends officials to the Assembly. Humans, dwarves, gnomes, halflings, and elves all hold recognised political representation. Officials are elected from towns, farming districts, forest settlements, mountain communities, trade ports, and guild boroughs. The purpose of the Assembly is to represent the strongest qualities of each people: Humans provide civic administration, agriculture, law, and expansion planning Dwarves provide engineering, mining knowledge, fortification, and legal precision Gnomes provide invention, scholarship, banking, and magical craft Halflings provide agriculture, food supply, local mediation, and community organisation Elves provide forest stewardship, long-term planning, diplomacy, and higher magical guidance The head of government is the Presiding Voice of Windmere , elected by the Assembly from among its senior officials. The Presiding Voice directs debate, signs laws, oversees diplomacy, and represents the state in formal negotiations. Windmere government is structured, wealthy, and debate-heavy. Laws are passed through negotiation between racial blocs, landholding interests, guilds, ports, and rural districts. Dominant Peoples ¶ The Windmere Assembly is home to humans, dwarves, gnomes, halflings, and elves. Humans form the largest population and dominate many farming towns, coastal settlements, civic offices, and trade routes. Dwarves live mainly near the mountain edges, fortified towns, stoneworks, foundries, and road-building districts connected to The Anvilspine Range and Barak Thuldren. Gnomes are concentrated in workshop towns, universities, counting houses, magical craft guilds, clockwork halls, and port districts. Halflings are common in the richest farming areas, orchard settlements, river villages, vineyard lands, and food markets. Elves live mainly in the southern forests, older groves, river estates, magical enclaves, and diplomatic districts. Their presence gives the Assembly strong influence in forestry, land management, and magical education. Region and Biome ¶ The Windmere Assembly sits in the Windmere Basin, on the eastern side of Arkhaven, near the cape and the eastern coast. It has access to the sea and to the waters of the Godscar , giving it strong maritime, river, and coastal trade potential. The state lies south of both Khuldovar and the Dornhal Empire , where the mountain systems descend and meet around the middle of the Windmere Basin. Rivers from the Anvilspine Range and Barak Thuldren flow down into Windmere, enriching the basin, feeding its farmland, and linking the Assembly to the dwarven highlands without placing it between the two dwarven states. The land is greener, warmer, and more fertile than much of the north. It consists of lush grassy plains, productive farmland, broad river valleys, orchards, vineyards, low hills, and increasingly dense forest in the south. The southern forests are cooler, older, and more elven-influenced. The central basin is dominated by farms, market towns, roads, and estates. The coastal cape contains ports, fisheries, shipyards, lighthouse towns, and fortified sea walls. Culture ¶ Windmere culture is prosperous, civic-minded, multi-racial, and land-conscious. The people value cooperation, property, trade, local identity, education, good food, and public debate. The Assembly has a strong culture of compromise. Humans, dwarves, gnomes, halflings, and elves live under one political structure, and each people maintains its own customs while contributing to the wider state. The wealth of the land shapes social life. Good farmland brings status, and families with fertile estates hold major influence. Landowners, millers, vintners, brewers, livestock holders, orchard masters, and river merchants carry significant power in rural politics. Windmere towns are cleaner, richer, and better supplied than settlements in harsher regions. Public granaries, stone roads, assembly halls, guildhouses, schools, bathhouses, gardens, mills, bridges, and river docks are common signs of civic investment. The state is known for harvest fairs, river markets, mixed-race civic festivals, public feasts, orchard rites, trade congresses, and formal debate days. Unlike more militarised or survival-focused states, Windmere’s identity is based on abundance and the management of abundance. Religion and Magic ¶ Religion in Windmere is diverse. Humans worship gods of harvest, law, craft, trade, family, safe travel, and sea passage. Dwarves honour gods of stone, forge, oath, and clan. Gnomes favour gods of invention, knowledge, luck, and clever craft. Halflings worship hearth, harvest, food, protection, and community deities. Elves honour the Seldarine, forest spirits, ancestral groves, and powers of nature and magic. Magic is present at a moderate to high level, depending on region and people. Elven communities use magic for forest stewardship, healing, wards, and long-term land protection. Gnomish settlements use magic for invention, construction, alchemy, clockwork, and civic convenience. Dwarven rune-workers apply magic to roads, bridges, locks, waterworks, and defensive architecture. Human and halfling communities use magic mainly for agriculture, healing, weather signs, food preservation, and trade. Magic in Windmere is regulated by local charters and Assembly law. Spellcasters are expected to register work that affects land, waterways, public roads, large buildings, or trade infrastructure. Tensions ¶ The main internal tension is wealth inequality. The land is richer than the north, and families with fertile estates control more money, food, and influence than poorer citizens, port workers, mountain-edge communities, and landless labourers. The second tension is representation. Each people has a recognised place in the Assembly, but disputes arise over voting weight, district borders, guild influence, and whether population, wealth, or racial balance should matter most. The third tension is land use. Humans and halflings push for more farming, dwarves push for roads and stoneworks, gnomes push for workshops and experimental districts, and elves push to preserve southern forests and old groves. These disputes are handled through law, but they remain constant.
docs.title: Windmere Assembly

docs.text: The Windmere Assembly is a wealthy, multi-racial state on the eastern cape of Arkhaven , built from human, dwarven, gnomish, halfling, and elven settlements. It is a fertile coastal assembly-state where rich grasslands, southern forests, mountain-fed rivers, and sea access have created one of the more prosperous societies on the continent. The Assembly is defined by shared government, productive land, racial cooperation, and commercial wealth. Its people are richer than most northern populations because the soil is better, the climate is kinder, and landowners with good farmland hold significant economic power.
docs.title: Windmere Assembly

docs.text: The Windmere Assembly is governed by an elected representative body known as the Grand Assembly of Windmere . Each major people of the state sends officials to the Assembly. Humans, dwarves, gnomes, halflings, and elves all hold recognised political representation. Officials are elected from towns, farming districts, forest settlements, mountain communities, trade ports, and guild boroughs. The purpose of the Assembly is to represent the strongest qualities of each people: Humans provide civic administration, agriculture, law, and expansion planning Dwarves provide engineering, mining knowledge, fortification, and legal precision Gnomes provide invention, scholarship, banking, and magical craft Halflings provide agriculture, food supply, local mediation, and community organisation Elves provide forest stewardship, long-term planning, diplomacy, and higher magical guidance The head of government is the Presiding Voice of Windmere , elected by the Assembly from among its senior officials. The Presiding Voice directs debate, signs laws, oversees diplomacy, and represents the state in formal negotiations. Windmere government is structured, wealthy, and debate-heavy. Laws are passed through negotiation between racial blocs, landholding interests, guilds, ports, and rural districts.

docs.text: The Windmere Assembly is home to humans, dwarves, gnomes, halflings, and elves. Humans form the largest population and dominate many farming towns, coastal settlements, civic offices, and trade routes. Dwarves live mainly near the mountain edges, fortified towns, stoneworks, foundries, and road-building districts connected to The Anvilspine Range and Barak Thuldren. Gnomes are concentrated in workshop towns, universities, counting houses, magical craft guilds, clockwork halls, and port districts. Halflings are common in the richest farming areas, orchard settlements, river villages, vineyard lands, and food markets. Elves live mainly in the southern forests, older groves, river estates, magical enclaves, and diplomatic districts. Their presence gives the Assembly strong influence in forestry, land management, and magical education.

docs.text: The Windmere Assembly sits in the Windmere Basin, on the eastern side of Arkhaven, near the cape and the eastern coast. It has access to the sea and to the waters of the Godscar , giving it strong maritime, river, and coastal trade potential. The state lies south of both Khuldovar and the Dornhal Empire , where the mountain systems descend and meet around the middle of the Windmere Basin. Rivers from the Anvilspine Range and Barak Thuldren flow down into Windmere, enriching the basin, feeding its farmland, and linking the Assembly to the dwarven highlands without placing it between the two dwarven states. The land is greener, warmer, and more fertile than much of the north. It consists of lush grassy plains, productive farmland, broad river valleys, orchards, vineyards, low hills, and increasingly dense forest in the south. The southern forests are cooler, older, and more elven-influenced. The central basin is dominated by farms, market towns, roads, and estates. The coastal cape contains ports, fisheries, shipyards, lighthouse towns, and fortified sea walls.

docs.text: Zul’Akari Clans ¶ The Zul’Akari Clans are a confederation of jungle, marsh, and lake-dwelling peoples in the north-west of Arkhaven . They are difficult to conquer due to the density of their terrain, the danger of local wildlife and monsters, and the defensive knowledge of the clans who live there. Government ¶ Zul’Akari is governed by a council of elders representing the largest and most influential peoples within the region. These elders act as clan leaders and are advised by shamans, oracles, and other spiritual figures. Leadership is not fully centralised. The balance of power between the clans can shift depending on population, military strength, religious influence, and alliances between groups. Dominant Peoples ¶ The main peoples of Zul’Akari include: Tabaxi Batiri goblins Yuan-ti Purebloods Salamanders Lizardfolk Other minor groups, beasts, and rumoured monster-kin are believed to exist deeper within the jungles and marshes. Region and Biome ¶ Zul’Akari lies in the north-western reaches of Arkhaven. Its landscape is made up of dense jungle, wetlands, marshes, rivers, and access to a massive freshwater lake. The environment is humid, dangerous, and difficult for outsiders to navigate or occupy. Culture ¶ Zul’Akari culture is clan-based, territorial, and strongly tied to the land. Each people maintains its own customs, traditions, and social structures, though the clans will cooperate when facing external threats. Ancient ruins, dungeons, and lost sites are usually treated as sacred places rather than abandoned structures. Outsiders who attempt to loot them are likely to be treated as enemies. The clans also trade with the Free Peoples of Kharad in the Kharad Wildlands, particularly with goliath rulers and Loxodon communities. Religion and Magic ¶ Religion is important throughout Zul’Akari, but it varies between peoples. Different clans worship gods, spirits, ancestors, or powers associated with their own traditions. Shamans and oracles play a major role in advising leaders, interpreting omens, and maintaining spiritual authority. Magic is used by those races and individuals capable of it. The region’s ancient ruins are believed to contain powerful artifacts, forgotten spells, and other dangerous magical remnants. Tensions ¶ There are ongoing tensions between the ruling clans, especially as each group competes for influence within the council. Despite this, external threats usually force cooperation. The main outside pressures come from the Haskarn Freeholds, who are human expansionists, and the Eldermarch Court, whose northern jungle-themed elves have their own interests in the region.

docs.text: Ithralen ¶ Ithralen is a scriptor town within the Court of Thalóriel , built around copy-halls, oath courts, dormitory cloisters, and Lanthir Súranel . Lanthir Súranel is the public elven name of the town’s scriptor college, usually translated into Common as the College of the Witnessed Word . Its name carries the sense of speech heard under oath, written before witnesses, and preserved without adornment. The college trains elven scriptors appointed through the Scriptor Compact. Students learn languages, temple law, religious history, miracle investigation, anti-forgery methods, archival magic, and the discipline of recording what was said rather than what would be easier to believe. Ithralen is quiet, exacting, and difficult to impress. A careless claim in the morning can become an examination by afternoon, and every chapel bell, lecture hall, and ink-room exists to remind students that poor records can become wars.

docs.text: New Meritus ¶ New Meritus is the capital city of the Republic of Havenor , built around the protected harbour where the Ark made landfall and now rests at Founding Quay . The city was named by the first Arkborne settlers in memory of Meritus , the eastern homeland they left behind after the Angel’s Command. To its defenders, the name honours survival, duty, and the preservation of human civilisation. To its critics, it reveals the ambition of the first settlers: they did not merely seek refuge in Arkhaven, they intended to plant a new version of the old world upon it. New Meritus is the civic heart of Havenor. The Mariner’s Senate meets here, close to the Ark, the First Manifest, the Oath Deck, and the working docks that still define Havenori politics. It is not a polished capital in the style of the Vermillion Crown. It is a busy harbour city of shipwrights, fishers, senators, clerics, guilds, old Ark families, ropewalks, timber yards, shrines, fish markets, taverns, public votes, and hard argument. Founding Quay is both shrine and workplace. Pilgrims come to see the preserved Ark, senators swear oaths within sight of it, guilds trace their authority back to the first professions aboard it, and ordinary dockworkers move cargo beneath its shadow. The city’s greatest tension is memory. New Meritus teaches every citizen that Havenor began with courage, divine warning, and impossible survival. Older peoples of Arkhaven often tell the same story differently, seeing the city as the first stone of human expansion, land claim, and unequal settlement.

docs.text: Caer Oryn ¶ Caer Oryn is the capital city of The Vermillion Crown , and one of the wealthiest and most politically important cities in Arkhaven . Caer Oryn sits on the River Oryn , which runs through the lower parts of the city before continuing west toward a great lake and the western waters of the Godscar . Capital of the Crown ¶ Caer Oryn sits at the heart of Vermillion power, serving as the seat of government, taxation, military authority, trade control, education, civic administration, and noble influence. Its power reaches far beyond the city because the Crown controls movement through the Godscar and the Crimson Chain. The city is walled, but not completely enclosed. Its strongest walls protect the main approaches, higher districts, military roads, and administrative heart of the city, while parts of the riverfront remain more open and heavily watched through quays, chain gates, patrol posts, and customs houses. The lower districts sit along the water. They contain the docks, warehouses, river labour offices, markets, workshops, modest housing, and much of the daily trade that keeps Caer Oryn alive. Farther from the river, the land rises toward the main keep. The Lord Protector’s seat stands on a hilltop above the city, removed from the noise of the waterfront and visible from many of the roads leading into Caer Oryn. Even the poorer districts are maintained, patrolled, educated, and economically functional. Caer Oryn has no true peasant quarter within its walls. Poverty exists, but it is managed through public labour, ration systems, civic schools, temple support, employment registers, and strict urban administration. The city is known for guarded gates, controlled river access, regulated districts, wealthy high wards, and a political culture built around permission, rank, debt, favour, and surveillance. Morfael ¶ Morfael sits on the outer edge of Caer Oryn. It serves the capital through river labour, ferry crossings, customs work, storage yards, fish markets, repair trades, cheap lodging, pauper burials, and the less formal commerce that the upper city prefers to keep at arm’s length. Morfael is close enough to Caer Oryn to be watched and regulated, but distant enough to be treated as useful rather than prestigious. Main Districts ¶ The River Districts ¶ Docks, warehouses, river labour offices, markets, workshops, customs houses, taverns, modest housing, and the working life of the city. The River Districts are where most goods, workers, travellers, and river traffic first meet Caer Oryn’s systems of inspection and control. The Guild Quarter ¶ Merchant houses, banking halls, guild courts, toll registries, caravan offices, trade brokers, and commercial offices. The Guild Quarter turns trade into contracts, permits, credit, debt, and legal authority. The Academy Quarter ¶ Schools, colleges, libraries, officer academies, legal halls, map archives, and magical institutes. The Academy Quarter reflects the Crown’s belief that knowledge is most useful when taught, licensed, recorded, and put to state service. The Foundry Quarter ¶ Armouries, inspection yards, military workshops, controlled foundries, river-chain mechanisms, and state weapon houses. The Foundry Quarter is one of the most restricted working districts in the city, especially during periods of military preparation, civic inspection, or heightened security. The High Quarter ¶ Ministerial estates, noble homes, embassies, treasury halls, high courts, theatres, civic temples, and formal gardens. The High Quarter displays wealth through discipline, property, patronage, formal service, and proximity to power. The Hillkeep ¶ The hilltop seat of power. It contains the Lord Protector’s keep, command chambers, state vaults, national archives, high courts, and the main offices of the Civic Directorate. The Hillkeep dominates the city physically and politically. Even from the lower roads, its towers are a reminder that Caer Oryn is a capital before it is a home. Cadris' Day ¶ Cadris' Day is a public holiday held in Caer Oryn to celebrate Lord Protector Maeron Cadris' coup and the beginning of the modern Vermillion Crown. Officially, it is remembered as the day divided noble rule ended and the Crown was restored to strength, discipline, and purpose. Streets are dressed in Vermillion banners, civic schools hold public recitations, soldiers parade through the higher districts, and officials give speeches praising order, service, and loyalty to the state. In the wealthier districts, Cadris' Day is polished and formal. There are military displays, academy processions, public feasts, temple blessings, and carefully arranged celebrations beneath the eyes of the Civic Directorate. In the lower districts, the holiday is more mixed. Some people celebrate it honestly, especially those whose families prospered under Cadris' rule. Others treat it as a day to keep quiet, hang the right colours, say the right words, and avoid being noticed. The city calls it a celebration. Plenty of people understand it is also a reminder.

docs.text: Karthrest ¶ Karthrest is a Crown lock-city built where a set of engineered water stairs forces river traffic to slow, register, and pay before continuing through the central passage routes. Its streets are narrow, paved in dark stone, and numbered by district rather than named by local custom. Barges enter under painted signal arms, while customs officers record cargo marks from balconies above the lock basins. Function ¶ Karthrest exists to turn movement into revenue. The city houses toll courts, cargo ledgers, confiscation yards, bond houses, licensed pilot guilds, and barracks for the Passage Directorate. A merchant can lose a season here over a damaged seal, an unpaid fee, or a single missing name from a charter. Unlike Caer Oryn, Karthrest does not pretend to be the heart of the Crown. It is a counting machine with walls, bells, floodgates, clerks, chain crews, auditors, and soldiers. Civic Mood ¶ People in Karthrest speak in docket numbers, cargo weights, canal times, and family permits. Children grow up learning the sound of lock-bells before they learn old songs. The city is prosperous, but tense. Delayed boats crowd the holding quays, foreign captains curse in rented rooms, and locals know that small mistakes can become legal traps. Tensions ¶ Karthrest is hated by smugglers and quietly feared by honest traders. The Passage Directorate claims the city keeps the heartlands safe. Rivermen say it keeps the Crown rich. Both are true.

docs.text: Morfael ¶ Morfael is a riverside town attached to the outer edge of Caer Oryn , capital of The Vermillion Crown . It is close enough to feel the capital’s weight, but not close enough to share fully in its wealth or protection. Morfael exists because Caer Oryn needs river labour, ferry crossings, customs records, cheap storage, fish markets, repair yards, pauper burials, and people willing to do work the upper city prefers not to see. Morfael should feel wet, lived-in, useful, and watched. It is not lawless, but it is not cleanly ordered in the way Caer Oryn’s higher districts are. Outside the Walls ¶ Morfael sits beyond the strongest sections of Caer Oryn’s walls. It has watch posts, toll points, river chains, customs sheds, ferry yards, and patrol routes, but it does not have the same polished order as the capital proper. People come here when they need work, passage, cheap lodging, quiet trade, river access, or a place where the Crown is watching but not always listening closely. The town is crowded with boatmen, washerfolk, dock labourers, fishmongers, cart drivers, repair workers, petty merchants, shrine-keepers, guards, pilgrims, widows, ferrymen, and people who cannot afford to live properly inside Caer Oryn. The Waterways ¶ The River Oryn is the town’s reason for existing. Goods, passengers, ferries, barges, market boats, and official cargo all pass through Morfael’s stretch of the river. The same waterways also carry runoff, rumours, lost things, and whatever the capital would rather send downstream. Morfael is useful to the Crown, useful to merchants, useful to ferry crews, and useful to people who prefer not to pass through the most obvious gates. Known Establishments ¶ Chapel of the Last Lantern ¶ The Chapel of the Last Lantern is a small, practical chapel connected to The Final Journey . It serves drowned sailors, paupers, dock accidents, unidentified dead, and families too poor to pay for formal rites inside Caer Oryn. Its bell is old and cracked. Locals say it sounds different when rung for someone whose passing is uncertain. The chapel is not grand. It is a place of last prayers, body-washing, funeral candles, death records, shrouds, and quiet comfort for those who have nowhere more formal to go. The Lumenwell Shrine ¶ The Lumenwell Shrine is a small Selûnite alcove built into an old flood wall. A shallow basin holds river water, and locals leave candles, names, travel tokens, and prayers for safe passage. Sailors, ferrymen, widows, messengers, and travellers visit the shrine before night crossings or long roads. It is also a place where families quietly remember those who have not returned. The Black Eel Market ¶ The Black Eel Market is a cramped fish and salvage market near the lower river steps. Its stalls sell river fish, smoked eel, cheap knives, netting, hooks, repaired boots, recovered river goods, and things no one asks too many questions about. It is not openly advertised as a criminal place, but most locals know where it is, when to go, and which questions not to ask loudly. The Flood Steps ¶ The Flood Steps are broad stone steps where Morfael meets the river. Fisherfolk, laundresses, children, dockhands, ferrymen, and paupers use them every day. During flood season, the lower steps vanish beneath brown-green water. When the river is low, the stones are slick with algae, old rope marks, fish scales, and river mud. Harrowchain Ferry ¶ The Harrowchain Ferry links Morfael to the opposite bank and the road network beyond. It is used by labourers, cart drivers, messengers, discreet couriers, and those who would rather not pass through the most formal Crown gates. It is watched, but not always as closely as the capital’s main approaches. The Hook and Bell ¶ The Hook and Bell is a low tavern near the quay. It serves fish stew, sour beer, dockside gossip, and cheap beds. It is not safe, but it is useful. Vellum House ¶ Vellum House is a narrow records office where cargo manifests, letters, permits, witness statements, dockside contracts, and other papers are written for people who cannot read, cannot write, or cannot safely use more official channels. It is a useful place for those who need paperwork, copied records, or someone who understands how Morfael’s trade actually moves. Cairnwell Yard ¶ Cairnwell Yard is a repair yard for carts, barges, cracked wheels, pulley frames, chain posts, dock hoists, ferry fittings, and warehouse doors. It is one of Morfael’s practical working yards: loud, muddy, busy, and essential. Low Lantern Row ¶ Low Lantern Row is a narrow line of lodging houses, cheap rooms, widows’ rooms, rented storage, and small apothecary rooms. People stay here when they are passing through, hiding from debt, working temporary river jobs, or living too close to poverty to afford better rooms. Marrowgate Road ¶ Marrowgate Road climbs from Morfael toward the controlled outer approaches of Caer Oryn. City watch, Crown agents, tax carts, labour traffic, pilgrims, and official processions all use it. For Morfael locals, it is both a road to opportunity and a reminder that the capital is always uphill.

docs.text: Ossengard ¶ Ossengard is a fortress city on the hard road between the Crown’s interior estates and the scar-facing military corridors. It is built in stepped rings around a weather-beaten drill plateau. The lower ring holds armour stores, mule yards, oath houses, repair sheds, and inns for soldiers in transit. The upper ring belongs to officers, instructors, magistrates, and families whose children are being prepared for state service. Military Schooling ¶ Ossengard is known for the Crown’s harshest officer schools. Cadets come here to learn logistics, siege discipline, map reading, winter marching, bridge defence, and the art of holding a road after retreat would be easier. The city is full of practice towers, measuring posts, mock gates, signal fires, and old battle diagrams carved into classroom walls. Graduating from Ossengard carries prestige, but failing there leaves a mark that can follow a family for years. City Character ¶ Ossengard is orderly without being elegant. Its people prize punctuality, spare speech, polished boots, clean weapons, and written proof of authority. Taverns close early near the academy ring, and even private feasts tend to sound like briefings. Tensions ¶ The city produces loyal officers, but also ambitious ones. Some instructors believe Maeron Cadris saved the Crown. Others quietly worry that a state trained to obey a single ruler may forget how to survive him.

docs.text: Rhalstoke ¶ Rhalstoke is an industrial riverworks city where the Crown builds the chains, winches, bridge teeth, pump housings, and pressure wheels used across its controlled waterways. The city sits beside a fast bend of the River Oryn, where water power, imported ore, timber shipments, and state contracts meet in a constant grind of labour. Its skyline is not graceful. It is stacks, gantries, hoists, cranes, slate roofs, furnace sheds, and signal horns. Riverworks ¶ Rhalstoke does not simply make weapons. Its workshops produce the practical machinery that lets the Vermillion Crown control passage: lock gears, chain gate teeth, flood braces, wagon axles, river cranes, bridge pins, harbour pulleys, and iron fittings for military roads. The Armature Directorate keeps inspectors in the city at all times. Poor work is treated as sabotage if it reaches a bridge, gate, or crossing. Workers and Wards ¶ The people of Rhalstoke are skilled, blunt, and proud of useful craft. Guild families live beside contracted labourers, veteran machinists, charcoal burners, barge-haulers, apprentice engineers, and state auditors. The city has wealth, but it smells of hot metal, wet timber, oil, coal dust, and river mud. Tensions ¶ Rhalstoke knows how much of the Crown depends on its mechanisms. Workers grumble about long hours and Directorate oversight, but few are careless. A failed chain gate can drown a district, open a route to enemies, or ruin a family name overnight.

docs.text: Kelshara ¶ Kelshara is a neighbouring settlement north-east of Tethvale , set deeper into the rainforest where the canopy thickens and the old stone of the Veylrain Expanse rises through the roots. It belongs to the Veylrath Clans , but its reputation is less about trade and more about memory. Kelshara is known for historians, relic preservation, artifact restoration, and careful study of the ruins buried beneath the jungle. The settlement is built around a series of moss-covered terraces known as the Kethari Steps , though no one agrees who first carved them or why so many of the lower stones disappear during the wet season. Keepers of Memory ¶ Kelshara’s most respected people are not warriors or merchants, but ruin-wardens, oral historians, appraisers, restoration workers, and elders who know how to read age from stone, root, metal, and dust. Relics found across nearby clan lands are often brought here before they are kept, traded, returned, sealed, or destroyed. This does not make Kelshara a museum. The Veylrath do not treat old things as decoration. A relic is a question, a warning, a debt, or a danger until it has been properly understood. Restoration and Relics ¶ The settlement contains shaded workhouses where broken objects are cleaned, bound, studied, and repaired with bone tools, resin, river clay, woven fibre, and quiet magic. Some relics are restored so their purpose can be known. Others are repaired only enough to prove they should never be used again. Kelshara is unusually open to human scholars, provided they work through recognised hosts and respect Veylrath ruin law. A small number of human historians, appraisers, translators, and restoration workers live here under clan protection or long-standing scholar agreements. Seraya Venn is one such human scholar, known locally as a careful relic historian whose work with preserved artifacts has earned more trust than most outsiders receive. Scholar Law ¶ Kelshara does not welcome treasure hunters, but it does welcome serious study. Visitors may copy inscriptions, examine restored objects, consult oral histories, and work beside local appraisers when permission has been granted. What they may not do is remove relics from protected ruins, conceal dangerous finds, or treat old places as abandoned property. The settlement’s storytellers teach that memory is not harmless. Remembering the wrong thing too proudly can wake what should have stayed buried.

docs.text: Nareth Lo ¶ Nareth Lo is a Veylrath settlement further downriver from Tethvale , hidden in wet rainforest where the Saelun River feeds into warmer channels near the Lo-Varin Pools . The settlement is known for medicine, alchemy, fungi, rare jungle plants, antidotes, salves, poultices, and quiet healers who know which leaf saves a life and which one stops it. It belongs to the Veylrath Clans , but it draws visitors from many settlements because the jungle wounds everyone eventually. The Living Stores ¶ Nareth Lo is built around living gardens rather than open streets. Raised walkways pass between moss houses, drying racks, shaded pools, bark sheds, spore huts, and groves where plants are tied with coloured thread to mark their use and danger. Nothing here is treated as merely useful. A medicine may also be poison. A fungus may feed a fever, numb a wound, stain a spirit, or mark a path that should not be followed twice. Medicine and Alchemy ¶ The healers of Nareth Lo work with roots, flowers, bark, venom, mould, fruit, insects, river clay, and old Veylrath rites. They make fever draughts, antivenoms, wound pastes, sleep-smoke, climbing salves, rot cures, fungal lanterns, scent masks, and medicines used by hunters and river travellers across clan lands. Their alchemy is not clean or academic. It stains fingers, smells strongly, changes with rainfall, and depends on knowing when a plant was gathered, what grew beside it, and what was sung before it was cut. Clan Life ¶ Nareth Lo is quiet, careful, and deeply respected. Children are taught early not to touch bright caps, silver vines, sweet-smelling sap, or water that reflects the wrong colour. Visitors are watched closely, not out of hostility, but because ignorance kills quickly here. Those who listen are treated well. Those who steal from the gardens are rarely invited to explain themselves twice. The settlement trades medicine, preserved herbs, alchemical mixtures, healing charms, and specialist knowledge to other Veylrath communities, but some plants are never sold outside clan law.

docs.text: Tethvale ¶ Tethvale is one of the major river-trade settlements of the Veylrath Clans , built high among the rainforest canopy above the broad bends of the Saelun River . It is small by human city standards, but large by Tabaxi and Veylrath standards. It is not a city in the Crown sense. There are no straight roads, stone avenues, or walls pretending the jungle is something to be conquered. Tethvale is made from suspended platforms, rope bridges, carved living branches, watch-nests, woven lifts, river stairs, and timber halls built around trees too old for anyone sensible to cut. The settlement sits where several canopy trails meet the Saelun, making it one of the safest and most important navigation points in the north-eastern Veylrain Expanse. Kelshara lies to the north-east along older canopy paths, Vurokai lies south-west where the rainforest thins toward savannah, and Nareth Lo sits further downriver where the Saelun feeds into warmer wetland channels near the Lo-Varin Pools. Canopy and River ¶ Tethvale’s upper settlement belongs to the trees. Families, traders, navigators, storytellers, scouts, and river-speakers live among layered platforms hidden by leaves, moss, and hanging flowers. Below, the riverfront is busy with narrow boats, ferry lines, fish traps, cargo nets, raft pens, and guarded landing stages. Goods move upward by rope lift and pulley, while travellers are watched carefully before being allowed into the higher walkways. The Saelun River is treated as road, boundary, memory, and warning. Its seasonal floods decide when trade moves quickly and when the jungle closes around everyone. Trade and Navigation ¶ Tethvale is known for river pilots, map-keepers, ferry families, quiet carriers, and traders who understand which waters are safe after heavy rain. Foreign merchants are allowed here more often than in deeper Veylrath settlements, though never without guides. They trade metal tools, salt, cloth, medicines, carved goods, preserved fruit, feathers, river pearls, rare woods, and stories worth repeating. The Veylrath do not sell maps freely. A route learned from Tethvale is usually given as a spoken chain of warnings, landmarks, spirits, smells, and turns, because a drawn line does not tell you what is waiting beneath the water. Clan Life ¶ Tethvale is loud, watchful, and alive at nearly every hour. Children learn knots before letters, hunters sleep in shaded hammocks above the docks, and elders sit near the bridge-posts telling travellers which questions are foolish. The settlement is open by Veylrath standards, but it is not careless. Ruin relics are declared before entering, weapons are bound at the river stairs, and anyone travelling deeper into the Expanse leaves with a guide or not at all.

docs.text: Tethvale is one of the major river-trade settlements of the Veylrath Clans , built high among the rainforest canopy above the broad bends of the Saelun River . It is small by human city standards, but large by Tabaxi and Veylrath standards. It is not a city in the Crown sense. There are no straight roads, stone avenues, or walls pretending the jungle is something to be conquered. Tethvale is made from suspended platforms, rope bridges, carved living branches, watch-nests, woven lifts, river stairs, and timber halls built around trees too old for anyone sensible to cut. The settlement sits where several canopy trails meet the Saelun, making it one of the safest and most important navigation points in the north-eastern Veylrain Expanse. Kelshara lies to the north-east along older canopy paths, Vurokai lies south-west where the rainforest thins toward savannah, and Nareth Lo sits further downriver where the Saelun feeds into warmer wetland channels near the Lo-Varin Pools.
docs.title: Tethvale

docs.text: Tethvale’s upper settlement belongs to the trees. Families, traders, navigators, storytellers, scouts, and river-speakers live among layered platforms hidden by leaves, moss, and hanging flowers. Below, the riverfront is busy with narrow boats, ferry lines, fish traps, cargo nets, raft pens, and guarded landing stages. Goods move upward by rope lift and pulley, while travellers are watched carefully before being allowed into the higher walkways. The Saelun River is treated as road, boundary, memory, and warning. Its seasonal floods decide when trade moves quickly and when the jungle closes around everyone.
docs.title: Canopy and River

docs.text: Tethvale is known for river pilots, map-keepers, ferry families, quiet carriers, and traders who understand which waters are safe after heavy rain. Foreign merchants are allowed here more often than in deeper Veylrath settlements, though never without guides. They trade metal tools, salt, cloth, medicines, carved goods, preserved fruit, feathers, river pearls, rare woods, and stories worth repeating. The Veylrath do not sell maps freely. A route learned from Tethvale is usually given as a spoken chain of warnings, landmarks, spirits, smells, and turns, because a drawn line does not tell you what is waiting beneath the water.

docs.text: Vurokai ¶ Vurokai is a border settlement of the Veylrath Clans , built south-west of Tethvale , where the heavy rainforest thins toward savannah, open scrub, and long grass. It stands near the western reaches of the Mavren Flats , where jungle trails, hunting paths, and grassland routes meet. The settlement is smaller than Tethvale and less scholarly than Kelshara , but few places in the Veylrain Expanse are more respected by hunters. Vurokai is known for trackers, monster slayers, hide-workers, bowyers, scouts, and clan families who spend half their lives reading mud, broken grass, claw marks, feathers, dung, and silence. Edge of the Rainforest ¶ Vurokai is built low compared with most Veylrath settlements. Some homes sit in trees, but many are raised on heavy posts above the damp ground, facing outward toward the savannah rather than inward toward the deep jungle. Watch platforms stand above the grassline. Smoke signals, carved trail posts, bone charms, and hidden warning bells mark the approaches. The borderlands are rich hunting ground, but they are also dangerous. Beasts move between jungle and grassland with the seasons, and not all of them are natural. Hunters and Monster Slayers ¶ The hunters of Vurokai are not merely providers of food. They are scouts, wardens, guides, and the first defence against things that wander too close to clan settlements. They track river cats, horned grazers, venomous packs, canopy-stalkers, burrowing things, and older monsters that come out of ruined ground after heavy rain. A kill is respected, but a warning given in time is respected more. Vurokai teaches that the best hunter is not the one who spills the most blood, but the one who brings everyone home. Clan Life ¶ Vurokai is practical, blunt, and wary of soft hands. Visitors are judged by how they walk, how they listen, and whether they notice when the insects stop singing. Outsiders who boast rarely stay welcome for long. The settlement trades hides, teeth, bone tools, smoked meat, venoms, hunting charms, and monster signs to other Veylrath communities. It also sends trackers to settlements that cannot survive without them.

docs.text: Arkhaven Regions ¶ Arkhaven is divided into several major geographic regions. These regions are not political entities, but broad environmental zones that shape climate, trade, settlement patterns, warfare, and culture. Many states occupy portions of multiple regions, while some regions contain several competing powers. Among the Tabaxi and many older peoples of the continent, Arkhaven is also known as Ithrava , meaning "The Land That Breathes" . This name predates the arrival of the human Ark upon the eastern shores and remains especially common among the peoples of the Veylrain Expanse. Overview ¶ The continent is broadly divided into eight major regions: Region Characteristics Veylrain Expanse Tropical rainforests, wetlands, river deltas, lakes, and coastal jungles The Thornbelt Dry plains, scrublands, badlands, and frontier wilderness The Crimson Chain The fractured waterways and cliffs of the Godscar The Floodlands Arid basins, shallow rivers, seasonal floodplains, and dry scrublands Arkenfall Northern forests, lakes, and eastern coastal frontiers Windmere Basin Fertile lowlands, river valleys, and southern agricultural heartlands Veridian March Temperate forests, rolling hills, and mixed woodland realms The Silent Weald Ancient forests, forgotten ruins, and lands touched by the Green Silence States within Arkhaven ¶ Many states occupy portions of multiple regions, while some regions contain several competing powers. Veylrain Expanse ¶ The Veylrain Expanse dominates the northern coastline of Arkhaven and contains some of the continent's oldest and most dangerous rainforests. Among the Tabaxi, the Expanse is one of the places where the name Ithrava , "The Land That Breathes" , remains strongest in everyday speech. To them, the rainforest is not merely a region of Arkhaven, but proof that the land is alive, remembering, and still speaking through rain, root, river, and ruin. Dense jungle stretches from the western coast to the eastern sea, broken only by rivers, wetlands, lakes, and scattered highlands. Heavy rainfall throughout much of the year creates a humid environment where vegetation rapidly consumes abandoned structures and forgotten roads. The Expanse is home to several powerful tribal societies, including the Zul’Akari Clans , Myruun Clans , Veylrath Clans , and Jhakur Clans . The Myruun are part of the Veylrain Expanse, but occupy its scar-facing edge at the northern end of the Crimson Chain. Ancient ruins are common throughout the region. Many remain unexplored, while others are protected by local peoples who regard them as sacred sites rather than sources of treasure. The Thornbelt ¶ The Thornbelt occupies much of north-central Arkhaven. It is a broad region of dry grassland, scrubland, rocky plains, seasonal rivers, and scattered hills. Conditions become increasingly harsh toward the interior, where water and fertile ground become valuable strategic resources. The Thornbelt serves as a natural buffer between the jungle societies of the north and the more settled states further south. Most of the region is occupied by the Kharad Wildlands , though portions of the Haskarn Freeholds , The Eldermarch Court , and neighbouring frontier territories extend into its edges. Trade routes crossing the Thornbelt are vital to communication between eastern and western Arkhaven. The Crimson Chain ¶ The Crimson Chain is the most strategically important region on the continent. Formed by the navigable waterways and steep cliffs of The Godscar , it divides much of Arkhaven while simultaneously providing one of its most important transportation corridors. Large lakes, deep river channels, fortified crossings, cliff roads, and narrow passages dominate the landscape. The region takes its name from the chain-like sequence of waterways extending from north to south through the continent. The Vermillion Crown controls many of the major crossings and passage routes, while The Leridian Concord and Court of Thalóriel maintain strong interests in the region. The Crimson Chain also contains the greatest concentrations of known veinstone deposits. Most exposed veins have been heavily worked over many centuries. Remaining deposits often appear as faint red crystalline seams with occasional flecks of gold visible within fractured cliff faces. At its northern end, the Crimson Chain meets the jungles of the Veylrain Expanse, where the Myruun Clans occupy scar-facing rainforest territory between jungle, sea, and fractured waters. The Floodlands ¶ The Floodlands occupy the north-eastern interior of Arkhaven. Unlike the dense jungles of the Veylrain Expanse, the Floodlands are primarily arid basin country shaped by shallow rivers, dry scrub, exposed floodplains, pale grasslands, and seasonal watercourses. For much of the year, travel follows dry routes, low ridges, shallow channels, and hard ground. During seasonal floods, the same rivers can overflow violently, turning low areas into temporary marsh, cutting off settlements, and forcing movement onto raised paths or higher ground. The region is dominated by The Skeldic Concord , although neighbouring powers maintain influence around its borders. Fishing, seasonal river trade, monster hunting, and floodplain agriculture are important aspects of life throughout the region. Arkenfall ¶ Arkenfall forms the eastern frontier of northern Arkhaven. Its landscape consists of mixed forests, rugged coastlines, lakes, river valleys, and isolated uplands. While less densely forested than the Veylrain Expanse, it remains heavily wooded and relatively difficult to traverse. The region contains much of the territory of the Republic of Havenor and the eastern reaches of the Jhakur Clans . Historically, Arkenfall marked the frontier between expanding human settlement and the older peoples of the northern wilderness. Windmere Basin ¶ The Windmere Basin occupies much of south-eastern Arkhaven. Fed by rivers descending from both the Anvilspine Range and the mountains of the Dornhal Empire , it is one of the most fertile regions on the continent. The basin contains rich farmland, vineyards, orchards, river valleys, market towns, and major trade roads. The Windmere Assembly occupies much of the southern basin, while the Dornhal Empire and The Throne of Khuldovar control the surrounding highlands and mountain systems. Its wealth derives from agricultural abundance, trade, and access to both inland and coastal routes. Veridian March ¶ The Veridian March stretches across much of western and central Arkhaven. The region consists primarily of temperate forests, rolling hills, grasslands, rivers, and settled woodland.

docs.text: Meritus ¶ Meritus is the eastern continent from which the first Humans and Aasimar came to Arkhaven aboard the Ark. In the oldest human records, the continent is sometimes called Meridian . The name reflects the belief that Meritus was the centre of the known world, the fixed point from which all lands, seas, kingdoms, roads, and peoples were measured. That belief did not end when the Arkborne reached Arkhaven. Many early human settlers continued to treat Meritus as the true heart of civilisation and Arkhaven as a promised refuge, frontier, or inheritance. The Angel’s Command ¶ The departure from Meritus began with a vision given to a human oracle. The event is remembered in human religious history as The Angel’s Command . According to Arkborne tradition, a celestial messenger appeared to the oracle and warned that Meritus would face a disaster no army could defeat and no crown could command away. The oracle was instructed to build a single Ark, gather those who could preserve human civilisation, and sail west across the ocean toward a scarred land beyond the sea. The command was specific enough to be obeyed, but vague enough to be disputed for centuries. It did not clearly define who deserved to be saved, whether Meritus would fall completely, or whether those left behind were doomed. The Chosen Families ¶ The Aasimar noble houses later claimed that their celestial blood proved they were meant to interpret and fulfil the Angel’s Command. They took leading roles in funding, organising, guarding, and blessing the Ark. Priests, officers, shipmasters, scholars, craftspeople, soldiers, nobles, and selected families were gathered for the crossing as part of the Ark’s 1,000 passengers. After the landing in Arkhaven, many of the first land grants went to families who had been aboard the Ark, especially those who could claim descent from Ark captains, oracle-guardians, priests, officers, and Aasimar patrons. To their supporters, these families preserved human civilisation. To their critics, they used a divine warning to save themselves first. The Unknown East ¶ The current state of Meritus is unknown. No confirmed voyage has returned with reliable news. Some believe the continent was destroyed. Some believe it survived but changed beyond recognition. Others claim the foretold disaster never came, and that the Arkborne abandoned their homeland because frightened nobles mistook prophecy for certainty. Churches in Arkhaven preserve fragments of Meritian scripture. Noble houses keep genealogies, seals, coins, maps, ship records, and old titles from the eastern homeland. Sailors still tell stories of lights on the eastern horizon, impossible storms, dead ships, and voices speaking old human dialects over empty water. None of these stories have been confirmed. Meritus remains central to human origin, Aasimar legitimacy, and the contested meaning of the Arkfall.

docs.text: Black Keel Brotherhood ¶ Description ¶ The Black Keel Brotherhood is a loose maritime network of captains, smugglers, salvage crews, wreckers, privateers, dockside brokers, river pilots, and sailors who understand that law becomes flexible once land is out of sight. They are not quite pirates, not quite merchants, and not quite a navy. That is why they survive. On the surface, they move cargo, crew ships, recover wrecks, guide vessels through dangerous waters, and offer passage when legal routes are closed. In truth, they also smuggle goods, hide fugitives, broker ransoms, sell information, and move things that no official harbour wants recorded. They are strongest in Republic of Havenor , around coastal trade routes, island coves, lake settlements, river mouths, and the waterways of The Godscar . Purpose ¶ The Black Keel Brotherhood exists to keep people and cargo moving by water when law, war, tolls, blockades, or politics get in the way. They are useful to merchants, criminals, refugees, spies, nobles, pirates, and desperate towns that need food more than they need clean paperwork. A Brotherhood ship may be the safest passage available. It may also be the reason the harbour master has stopped asking questions. Rules ¶ A captain’s word given over water matters. A marked Brotherhood vessel is not to be raided by another Brotherhood crew. Spoils are divided by crew law, not noble title. Shipwrecked crews are ransomed, recruited, or released unless they have earned worse. Do not sell passengers to slavers, cults, or experimental mages. Never ask too much about the cargo unless the answer will raise the price. Personality ¶ The Black Keel Brotherhood is rough, funny, dangerous, superstitious, and loyal in its own way. Its members drink with pirates, sell news to admirals, lie to customs officers, and still insist they are honest sailors. They respect nerve, competence, and anyone who pays on time. They do not respect people who think a seal, crown, or temple stamp means the sea will obey them.

docs.text: The Black Keel Brotherhood is a loose maritime network of captains, smugglers, salvage crews, wreckers, privateers, dockside brokers, river pilots, and sailors who understand that law becomes flexible once land is out of sight. They are not quite pirates, not quite merchants, and not quite a navy. That is why they survive. On the surface, they move cargo, crew ships, recover wrecks, guide vessels through dangerous waters, and offer passage when legal routes are closed. In truth, they also smuggle goods, hide fugitives, broker ransoms, sell information, and move things that no official harbour wants recorded. They are strongest in Republic of Havenor , around coastal trade routes, island coves, lake settlements, river mouths, and the waterways of The Godscar .
docs.title: Description

docs.text: The Black Keel Brotherhood exists to keep people and cargo moving by water when law, war, tolls, blockades, or politics get in the way. They are useful to merchants, criminals, refugees, spies, nobles, pirates, and desperate towns that need food more than they need clean paperwork. A Brotherhood ship may be the safest passage available. It may also be the reason the harbour master has stopped asking questions.
docs.title: Purpose

docs.text: A captain’s word given over water matters. A marked Brotherhood vessel is not to be raided by another Brotherhood crew. Spoils are divided by crew law, not noble title. Shipwrecked crews are ransomed, recruited, or released unless they have earned worse. Do not sell passengers to slavers, cults, or experimental mages. Never ask too much about the cargo unless the answer will raise the price.
docs.title: Rules

docs.text: The Black Keel Brotherhood is rough, funny, dangerous, superstitious, and loyal in its own way. Its members drink with pirates, sell news to admirals, lie to customs officers, and still insist they are honest sailors. They respect nerve, competence, and anyone who pays on time. They do not respect people who think a seal, crown, or temple stamp means the sea will obey them.
docs.title: Personality

docs.text: Free Road Alliance ¶ Description ¶ The Free Road Alliance is a loose agreement between towns, road wardens, caravan houses, guild councils, minor lords, independent ports, bridge-keepers, and settlements that are tired of being crushed between stronger powers. They are not a kingdom. They are not an army in the proper sense. They are a promise that certain roads, markets, bridges, ferries, and border towns should stay open, even when rulers would rather close them. The Alliance is strongest along trade routes, frontier roads, Godscar crossings, and places where local people would otherwise be swallowed by the ambitions of larger states. They are common around the Crimson Chain, the Thornbelt, Republic of Havenor , The Vermillion Crown , The Leridian Concord , and smaller settlements that need neutrality to survive. It sounds noble. Sometimes it is. Other times it is just a lot of frightened towns agreeing that being useful is safer than being conquered. Purpose ¶ The Free Road Alliance exists to keep movement possible across Arkhaven. They protect neutral roads, escort caravans, ransom travellers, maintain bridges, settle toll disputes, and try to stop local conflicts turning into full annexations. A village under the Alliance seal is not always safe, but it is harder to erase quietly. Rules ¶ An Alliance road is neutral unless an army breaks that neutrality first. A marked town must shelter lawful travellers, wounded envoys, and registered caravans when it can. Banditry, false tolls, hostage-taking, bridge-burning, and forged road charters are treated as crimes against all members. The Alliance does not overthrow states. It survives by being useful enough that even powerful rulers hesitate before crushing it. Members may argue, bribe, stall, and scheme, but they do not betray the road itself. Personality ¶ The Free Road Alliance is stubborn, practical, bureaucratic, and constantly arguing with itself. Its people like ledgers, seals, road markers, escort contracts, witness stones, and emergency councils that go on far too long. They are not romantic heroes. They are mayors, wardens, merchants, ferrymen, clerks, and tired soldiers trying to keep the next bridge standing. When they work, nobody notices. When they fail, towns burn and the roads close.

docs.text: The Ashen Vow ¶ Description ¶ The Ashen Vow is a militant holy order made up of paladins, priests, exorcists, temple guards, battlefield confessors, monster hunters, and soldiers who have seen what faith can become when it is used badly. They were shaped by the memory of the War of the False Saints. To them, false miracles are not harmless lies. They are the first step toward mobs, purges, broken kingdoms, and another continent-wide disaster. The Ashen Vow are not part of any single church or state, though many temples tolerate them and many rulers use them when it suits. They are called when cults gather, saints are declared too quickly, relics start speaking, the dead do not stay buried, or a village begins worshipping something it found beneath the ground. They often cross paths with the Scriptor Compact, but they are not the same kind of people. Scriptors preserve doctrine and investigate records. The Ashen Vow are the ones sent when a door needs breaking. Purpose ¶ The Ashen Vow exists to stop faith being turned into a weapon again. They investigate false saints, miracle cults, undead outbreaks, fiendish influence, cursed relics, forbidden shrines, and religious movements that begin gathering swords before answers. At their best, they protect ordinary people from monsters wearing holy language. At their worst, they start seeing monsters everywhere. Rules ¶ No miracle is above examination. No prophet is above law. No temple may raise a private army without scrutiny. Do not destroy evidence unless leaving it intact would cause immediate harm. Accept surrender from the deceived. Show no mercy to those who knowingly manufacture miracles, saints, or relics to control the desperate. The Vow does not exist to punish doubt. It exists to punish corruption. Personality ¶ The Ashen Vow are severe, brave, suspicious, and difficult to relax around. They are respected by common folk who have seen cults take root, feared by priests with secrets, and watched carefully by rulers who do not like armed holy orders getting ideas. A good member of the Vow is disciplined, patient, and painfully honest. A bad one is only one bad vision away from a purge. That tension is what makes them useful and dangerous in equal measure.

docs.text: The Gilded Chain ¶ Description ¶ The Gilded Chain is a continent-spanning alliance of merchants, bankers, caravan masters, toll-brokers, warehouse owners, insurers, private guards, river factors, and mercenary captains. On the surface, they are a respectable trade network. They move goods, guard roads, insure caravans, lend coin, secure ships, rebuild bridges, and make sure commerce survives war, bad weather, bandits, and politics. In truth, they are as much a power bloc as any court or army. They do not need to conquer a city if they can own its debt, its grain stores, its river contracts, and the company paid to guard its gates. They are strongest wherever trade is difficult but necessary, especially around The Godscar , the Crimson Chain, The Vermillion Crown , The Leridian Concord , Republic of Havenor , and the routes crossing the Thornbelt. Purpose ¶ The Gilded Chain exists to control trade without openly ruling land. They keep roads, ports, ferries, markets, warehouses, and caravans working, but always with a price attached. A town protected by the Chain may be safer, richer, and better supplied than its neighbours. It may also find itself unable to make a single meaningful decision without checking the terms of a contract signed twenty years ago. Rules ¶ A signed contract matters. Breaking one without cause is treated worse than theft. Chain members do not raid marked caravans, ships, warehouses, or counting houses. Internal betrayal is punished harder than outside attack. Debt is a tool, not a tantrum. The Chain prefers leverage, dependency, and quiet pressure over pointless cruelty. Infrastructure is valuable. Bridges, roads, locks, docks, and ferries are not destroyed unless the profit has already been calculated. Coin is not the only currency. Favour, silence, safe passage, food, maps, escorts, and blackmail all spend well enough. Personality ¶ The Gilded Chain are polite, practical, patient, and quietly predatory. They dress well, keep records, honour deals, and smile while working out exactly how desperate someone is. They are not chaotic criminals. That would be too simple. They are reasonable people who believe morality is just another cost to be negotiated. A good Chain agent does not threaten a town. They explain what happens if the next grain convoy is delayed.

docs.text: The Lanternwise ¶ Description ¶ The Lanternwise are a loose network of informants, travellers, singers, scribes, scouts, old soldiers, river pilots, teachers, and ordinary people who make a habit of knowing things they probably should not. On the surface, they are harmless enough. They carry stories, news, warnings, letters, rumours, songs, and small acts of charity across Arkhaven. In truth, they are a quiet resistance against tyrants, false saints, slavers, cults, corrupt guilds, and rulers who think truth belongs only to them. They are not a formal rebellion. They do not hold land or march under one banner. Most members only know a handful of others, which is exactly the point. They are most active around the major roads, ports, crossings, and places where information is controlled, especially near The Godscar , the Crimson Chain, The Vermillion Crown , The Leridian Concord , Republic of Havenor , and the archive-towns watched by the Court of Thalóriel . Purpose ¶ The Lanternwise exist to keep people, stories, and warnings moving. They hide witnesses, move refugees, copy records before they vanish, expose false miracles, and make sure powerful people cannot simply erase what happened. To them, a burned village, a missing convoy, a forged confession, or a murdered scribe is not just another local tragedy. It is evidence. Rules ¶ The Lanternwise do not rule in their own name. They may interfere, expose, rescue, smuggle, or sabotage, but they do not crown kings or seize towns. They do not kill for convenience. Violence is used when there is no cleaner way to stop something worse. They preserve true accounts, even ugly ones. Names, maps, letters, songs, ledgers, and witness statements matter. They work in small cells. No member should know enough to bring the whole network down. They do not sell out the helpless. A person under Lanternwise protection is not a bargaining chip. Personality ¶ The Lanternwise are warm, nosy, stubborn, and difficult to pin down. They are the sort of people who ask too many questions, remember too many names, and turn up at exactly the wrong time for whoever is trying to keep something quiet. They prefer quiet interference over grand speeches. A good Lanternwise victory is usually one nobody notices until the prisoner is gone, the second copy survives, or the truth is already being sung three towns away.

docs.text: The Mercurial Blade ¶ Description ¶ The Mercurial Blade is a private order of mages, spies, duelists, illusionists, diviners, magical scholars, and agents who believe magic is too dangerous to be left entirely in the hands of kings, priests, armies, or universities. They are not a formal academy, though many of them were trained in one. They are not a simple spy network either, though they are very good at behaving like one. On the surface, the Mercurial Blade appears as patrons, tutors, court mages, duel instructors, translators, negotiators, and arcane consultants. Beneath that, they trade in magical knowledge, coded correspondence, discreet interventions, stolen research, and quiet corrections when powerful people become careless with spellcraft. They are most often found in cities where magic and politics overlap, especially around The Leridian Concord , The Vermillion Crown , Court of Thalóriel , and the larger ports of Republic of Havenor . Purpose ¶ The Mercurial Blade exists to keep dangerous knowledge moving, but not freely. They preserve spells, expose reckless magical research, steal dangerous texts before worse people can use them, and quietly remove mages who become a public problem. Their belief is simple enough. Magic should not belong to one throne. The problem is that they often believe it should belong to them instead. Rules ¶ No ruler owns a school of magic. A dangerous spell should be recorded before it is used. Magical disasters are to be contained before blame is assigned. Never reveal serious arcane knowledge to someone too ambitious, desperate, or stupid to survive it. A mage who hides catastrophic research becomes part of the problem. Subtlety first. Duels second. Fireballs last. Personality ¶ The Mercurial Blade are clever, sharp, arrogant, and difficult to trust completely. They like masks, coded letters, clean blades, hidden spellwork, and conversations where every sentence has three meanings. They are useful allies when the problem is magical, political, or both. They are dangerous enemies because they rarely look like enemies until the spell is already finished.

docs.text: The Veiled Path ¶ Description ¶ The Veiled Path is known across Arkhaven as a thieves’ guild, though even that may be too simple. On the surface, it is a continent-spanning criminal network of burglars, smugglers, fences, counterfeiters, cutpurses, dockside runners, corrupt clerks, safehouse keepers, and quiet brokers who can move stolen goods across borders better than most legal caravans. It is spoken of in ports, taverns, prisons, counting houses, gambling rooms, and alleyways where people know better than to say the name too loudly. No one agrees where it began. Havenor blames the pirate routes. The Crown blames Leridian agents. Leridia blames Crown corruption. Others say it is older than both and simply learned to wear whatever mask each city expected. That is as much as most people know. It is probably as much as they are meant to know. Purpose ¶ The Veiled Path exists to steal, smuggle, hide, move, and sell things that the lawful world cannot or will not touch. Coin, relics, letters, prisoners, poisons, names, maps, noble secrets, black-market goods, forged permits, and forbidden books all pass through its hands. To most people, it is just crime made organised. To criminals, it is something larger and less comfortable than that. Rules ¶ Do not steal from another marked member. Do not expose a safehouse. Do not speak the Path’s signs to law, crown, temple, scriptor, or torturer. Pay the veil-tithe. Never ask who sits at the end of the Path. A job may be refused, but a debt may not be forgotten. Personality ¶ The Veiled Path is charming, theatrical, secretive, and superstitious. Its members like coded phrases, hidden doors, marked coins, false names, and stories that contradict each other on purpose. Most people think they are just thieves. Most thieves hope that is true.
