docs.text: Veridian Conclave ¶ Description ¶ The Veridian Conclave is a loose order of druids, rangers, wardens, shamans, herbalists, beast-speakers, ruin-keepers, and land-priests who protect the living places of Arkhaven. They are not against civilisation. That would be too simple. They accept farms, roads, towns, trade, hunting, timber, and settlement when it is done with sense. What they oppose is stupidity. Poisoned rivers, sacred ruins treated as treasure houses, forests cut until the soil dies, mines dug into cursed seams, marshes drained without understanding them, and nobles who mistake ownership for permission. They are strongest in the Veridian March, the Veylrain Expanse, the Silent Weald, the Floodlands, the Kharad Wildlands , and around older elven territories where the land still remembers things people do not. Purpose ¶ The Veridian Conclave exists to stop civilisation and wilderness destroying each other. They watch for blight, poisoned waters, unnatural silence, dangerous growth, altered beasts, cursed ruins, and places where old magic has begun moving again. They do not protect nature because it is gentle. They protect it because when it breaks, people usually break with it. Rules ¶ The land is to be listened to before it is used. Sacred ruins are not abandoned property. Water, soil, forest, herd, and harvest matter more than the pride of a lord. A monster is not always an enemy. Sometimes it is a warning. Do not destroy what you do not understand unless it is already killing people. A Conclave warden serves the balance of a place before the politics of a border. Personality ¶ The Veridian Conclave is practical, suspicious, weather-beaten, and blunt. Its members are often calm in ways that annoy everyone else. They will let a council argue for hours and then say the river has already answered. They are patient with farmers, children, animals, and old roads. They are less patient with treasure hunters, careless mages, and rulers who think a map is the same thing as knowing a place.

docs.text: Caer Oryn & Morfael Gazetteer ¶ Player-facing gazetteer for Caer Oryn, capital of the Vermillion Crown, and Morfael, the river town pressed against its outer edge. Caer Oryn is the polished face of Vermillion power: a white-stone capital of bridges, permits, academies, soldiers, civic schools, toll offices, formal temples, river chains, and watched streets. It is wealthy, educated, organised, and proud of being all three. Its citizens are taught that prosperity comes from discipline, and that discipline requires schooling, service, law, and loyalty to the state. Morfael is what sits below that order. It is close enough to the capital to be controlled by it, but far enough downriver and downhill to be ignored when convenient. It exists because Caer Oryn needs river labour, ferry crossings, customs records, cheap storage, fish markets, pauper burials, repair yards, and people willing to do work the upper city prefers not to see. This gazetteer is written for players. It contains public knowledge, visible institutions, common local texture, and places characters might reasonably know about or visit. It does not include hidden histories, DM-only explanations, encounter tables, stat blocks, or secret faction structures. To its enemies, the Crown is a state that has turned geography into a weapon and movement into obedience. The state is ruled by Lord Protector Maeron Cadris , whose full formal title is Lord Protector Maeron Cadris, Guardian of the Godscar, Warden of the Crimson Chain, Supreme Marshal of the Crown Armies, Keeper of Caer Oryn . Cadris took power twenty years ago through a coup. Before his rule, authority was divided between noble houses, military officers, trade officials, and regional governors. His rule ended that divided balance and replaced it with a centralised state built around discipline, education, military readiness, surveillance, and public loyalty. Many citizens believe Cadris saved the Crown from noble paralysis and made it strong enough to survive its enemies. Others keep quieter views. In the Vermillion Crown, silence is often treated as good judgement. The Civic Directorate ¶ The Civic Directorate is the central ruling system created after Maeron Cadris took power. It controls law, education, military administration, movement, taxation, infrastructure, state security, and the regulation of Godscar passage. To outsiders it can feel like a maze of seals and offices. To loyal citizens it is the machine that keeps roads open, schools funded, bridges guarded, locks working, and enemies contained. The Passage Directorate controls roads, rivers, bridges, locks, tolls, travel permits, licensed ports, Crimson Chain movement, and Godscar crossings. The Treasury Directorate controls taxation, state coinage, merchant charters, Crown contracts, banking oversight, and toll revenue. The Directorate of Instruction controls public schooling, academies, civic education, officer training, approved histories, legal education, and scholarship grants. The Armature Directorate controls military supply, armouries, officer postings, fortress planning, strategic weapons, and state weapons production. The Surveyor Directorate controls maps, land records, censuses, water routes, mineral claims, Godscar studies, and infrastructure planning. Most citizens do not interact with every branch, but almost everyone lives under the weight of at least one of them. Caer Oryn: Capital of the Crown ¶ Caer Oryn is a vast hexagonal city of white stone built around the River Oryn. The river passes through the capital from east to west, beneath six monumental bridges, before continuing toward Lake Tharne and the western waters of the Godscar. The city’s hexagonal design is deliberate: six sides, six major approaches, six fortified civic divisions, and six great bridges over the River Oryn. Even visitors who know nothing of Vermillion politics can see that Caer Oryn was built to express control. The city is walled, but not simply sealed shut. Its strongest walls protect the main approaches, higher districts, military roads, and administrative centres. The riverfront is more open, because commerce demands movement, but it is heavily watched through quays, chain gates, patrol posts, customs houses, permit offices, and Crown officials who monitor what enters and leaves by water. The lower districts contain docks, warehouses, markets, river labour offices, workshops, taverns, modest housing, public schools, and most of the working life of the city. These areas are busy, useful, and tightly managed rather than abandoned. Farther from the water, the city rises into wealthier and more controlled districts. At the centre stands the Crownward: the seat of command, law, archives, vaults, and national administration. Caer Oryn has no true peasant quarter within its walls. Poverty exists, but it is managed through public labour, ration systems, civic schools, temple support, employment registers, and strict urban administration. This does not make the city kind. It makes the city efficient. Districts and Civic Divisions of Caer Oryn ¶ The Outer Wards ¶ Residential districts, workshops, public schools, warehouses, river labour offices, markets, and modest but stable housing. The Outer Wards are where most ordinary citizens encounter the Crown’s promise: work, school, patrols, paperwork, and the expectation that useful people should remain useful. The Guild Quarter ¶ Merchant houses, banking halls, guild courts, toll registries, caravan offices, trade brokers, and commercial offices. Wealth moves through the Guild Quarter in ledgers before it moves in coin. A damaged seal, unclear charter, or unpaid fee can trap a merchant here longer than a broken axle. The Academy Quarter ¶ Schools, colleges, libraries, officer academies, legal halls, map archives, and magical institutes. Caer Oryn invests heavily in education because educated citizens become effective clerks, officers, engineers, merchants, surveyors, lawyers, administrators, and mages. Credentials matter here almost as much as blood. The Foundry Quarter ¶ Armouries, inspection yards, military workshops, controlled foundries, river-chain mechanisms, and state weapon houses. The Foundry Quarter does not exist only to make blades. It supports the machinery of a passage state: chains, locks, hoists, bridge fittings, signal devices, and military equipment. The High Quarter ¶ Ministerial estates, noble homes, embassies, treasury halls, high courts, theatres, civic temples, and formal gardens. The High Quarter is wealthy, polished, and careful. Even celebration here looks inspected. The Crownward ¶ The central seat of power. It contains the Lord Protector’s palace and keep, the highest courts, national archives, command chambers, state vaults, and the main offices of the Civic Directorate. Citizens may speak of the Crownward with pride, but most do not expect to enter it without cause. Cadris' Day ¶ Cadris’ Day is a public holiday held in Caer Oryn to celebrate Lord Protector Maeron Cadris’ coup and the beginning of the modern Vermillion Crown. Officially, it is remembered as the day divided noble rule ended and the Crown was restored to strength, discipline, and purpose. Streets are dressed in Vermillion banners, civic schools hold public recitations, soldiers parade through the higher districts, and officials give speeches praising order, service, and loyalty to the state. In the wealthier districts, Cadris’ Day is polished and formal. There are military displays, academy processions, public feasts, temple blessings, and carefully arranged celebrations beneath the eyes of the Directorate. In the lower districts, the holiday is more mixed. Some people celebrate it honestly, especially those whose families prospered under Cadris’ rule. Others treat it as a day to keep quiet, hang the right colours, say the right words, and avoid being noticed. The city calls it a celebration. Plenty of people understand it is also a reminder. Other Major Cities of the Vermillion Crown ¶ Caer Oryn is the capital, but it is not the only city that matters. Karthrest is a fortified lock-city where engineered water stairs force river traffic to slow, register, and pay before continuing through Crown-controlled passage routes. It is a counting machine with walls, bells, floodgates, clerks, chain crews, auditors, and soldiers. Ossengard is a fortress city and officer-school centre on the hard road between the Crown’s interior estates and scar-facing military corridors. It is known for harsh military schooling, logistics training, siege discipline, map reading, winter marching, and the art of holding a road after retreat would be easier. Rhalstoke is an industrial riverworks city that builds the chains, gears, bridge parts, pump housings, gate mechanisms, lock teeth, flood braces, pulleys, and iron fittings used across Crown-controlled routes. It smells of hot metal, wet timber, oil, coal dust, and river mud. Together, these cities show what the Vermillion Crown values: movement, discipline, machinery, education, military readiness, and control. Morfael: The Wet Edge of the Capital ¶ Morfael is a river town attached to the outer edge of Caer Oryn. It is close enough to feel like part of the capital, but far enough outside the main walls to be treated differently. The town sits downstream of the city, where the River Oryn runs west toward Lake Tharne. Morfael grew where the capital did not want to look too closely. Smaller channels, drainage cuts, service roads, spillways, poorer river land, and half-official storage all collect here before the water reaches the lake. Morfael is not lawless, but it is not Caer Oryn either. It has watch posts, toll points, river chains, customs sheds, patrol routes, and Crown officers. It does not have the same clean order as the higher districts inside the capital. People come to Morfael when they need work, passage, cheap lodging, river access, or a place where the city’s rules are present but less polished. The town is crowded with boatmen, washerfolk, dock labourers, fishmongers, cart drivers, sewer workers, petty merchants, shrine-keepers, beggars, guards, pilgrims, and people who cannot afford to live properly inside Caer Oryn. Morfael should feel wet, lived-in, poor in places, useful to everyone, and trusted by no one. It is close to power, but rarely protected by it. Sites of Morfael ¶ The Flood Steps ¶ Broad stone steps where the river meets the town. Fisherfolk, laundresses, children, dockhands, ferrymen, paupers, and market runners use these steps every day. During flood season, the lower steps vanish under brown-green water. Locals treat the Flood Steps as ordinary, which is exactly why anything strange there becomes everyone’s business. The Black Eel Market ¶ A cramped fish and salvage market near the Flood Steps. Its stalls sell river fish, smoked eel, cheap knives, netting, hooks, repaired boots, recovered river goods, broken tools, and cheap food. It is noisy, practical, and crowded enough that visitors can miss half of what matters. Chapel of the Last Lantern ¶ A small, practical chapel connected to The Final Journey . It serves drowned sailors, paupers, dock accidents, unidentified dead, grieving families, and those too poor to pay for formal rites in Caer Oryn. Its bell is old and cracked. Locals know its sound well. Lumenwell Shrine ¶ A small Selûnite alcove built into an old flood wall. A shallow basin holds river water. Sailors, ferrymen, widows, messengers, and travellers leave candles here before night crossings or long roads. It matters because ordinary people ask for safe passage here, write names of the missing, leave letters for those who may never return, and sit with uncertainty. The Red Lockhouse ¶ A Crown-controlled customs and lock office near the canal mouth. It handles tolls, cargo seals, river permits, lock schedules, late fees, and arguments about missing stamps. Most Morfael residents dislike dealing with it, but nearly everyone depends on it working. Harrowchain Ferry ¶ A chain ferry linking Morfael to the opposite bank and several river paths used by labourers, messengers, market folk, and people avoiding the longer official crossings. It is slow, noisy, useful, and part of the town’s daily rhythm. The Hook and Bell ¶ A low tavern near the quay. It serves fish stew, sour beer, dockside gossip, and cheap beds. It is not refined, but it is useful. In Morfael, that is often enough. Vellum House ¶ A narrow records office where cargo manifests, letters, invoices, permits, dockside contracts, and discreet copies are written for people who cannot read or cannot easily deal with Caer Oryn’s formal offices. Cairnwell Yard ¶ A repair yard for carts, barges, cracked wheels, pulley frames, chain posts, hooks, dock hoists, and practical metalwork. If something breaks in Morfael and cannot be carried to Caer Oryn, it usually passes through Cairnwell Yard. Low Lantern Row ¶ A narrow row of lodging houses, cheap rooms, widows’ rooms, and rented storage. It is cramped, damp, and never entirely quiet. Marrowgate Road ¶ The road climbing from Morfael toward the controlled outer approaches of Caer Oryn. City watch, Crown agents, tax carts, legal messengers, military clerks, and official processions use this road more than locals do. Public Faces of Morfael ¶ Cerys Varrow is the Crown-appointed reeve of Morfael. She manages taxes, dock complaints, street repairs, official notices, and the difficult work of answering to Caer Oryn while living among people who resent her authority. Watch-Corporal Dannel Strake is a lower-town watch corporal. He is tired, cautious, and not as corrupt as people assume. He wants order first and truth second, which makes him frustrating but not useless. Sister Halva Dorn is a dwarf lay-priest of the Chapel of the Last Lantern. She tends the poor dead, drowned sailors, unnamed bodies, and families who cannot afford the upper city. She is stern, compassionate, and difficult to intimidate. Eira Lorne keeps Lumenwell Shrine. She is not a grand priestess; she cleans the basin, lights candles, records names, comforts families, and remembers which riverfolk have not come home. Old Pell is the ferryman of Harrowchain Ferry. He knows the river better than the town watch knows its streets, speaks slowly, and notices everything. Mara Venn is a fishmonger at the Black Eel Market. She is loud, practical, and protective of local children. She knows who belongs in Morfael and who walks like they are pretending to belong. Joric Marn is a customs factor at the Red Lockhouse. He keeps records, stamps permits, and has mastered the official art of not understanding more than he is paid to understand. Elian Marr is a retired lock engineer. He knows old waterworks, service routes, and outdated mechanisms better than many current officials. Maelis Wren is an apothecary of Low Lantern Row. She sells poultices, sleep draughts, fever tinctures, dockhand liniment, and the kind of quiet help poor people seek before risking official attention. Law, Order, and Daily Control ¶ Caer Oryn’s law is written, recorded, witnessed, and procedural. A document can matter more than a sword if the seal is correct. A missing seal can make honest cargo look criminal. A bad ledger entry can stall a family business for months. Morfael’s law is rougher. The watch knows many offenders by name, but the town also knows when the watch chooses not to see something. Serious matters involving Crown officers, customs records, foreign travellers, military cargo, or suspicious river traffic can be pulled into Caer Oryn’s systems quickly. Once that happens, Morfael rarely hears the full story again. The Passage Directorate is the branch ordinary travellers most often fear. It controls permits, crossings, lock schedules, tolls, licensed river movement, and the practical right to pass from one place to another without being stopped. The public lesson is simple: movement through the Vermillion Crown is possible, profitable, and protected, but it is never truly free. Economy and Trade ¶ Caer Oryn turns movement into power. Its wealth comes from river tolls, merchant charters, legal authority, civic schooling, military administration, academy training, public contracts, bridge control, lock control, customs enforcement, and the ability to make everyone else’s passage depend on Crown systems. Morfael survives on the physical work behind that wealth. Fish are smoked. Ropes are tarred. Ferries are poled. Carts are repaired. Bodies are washed. Letters are written. Cargo is shifted. Drains are cleared. Barges are patched. Names are remembered. The capital counts value in ledgers. Morfael counts it in favours, names, routes, and who will still open a door after dark. Religion and Magic ¶ The Vermillion Crown worships many gods, especially those associated with law, victory, wealth, civilisation, knowledge, craft, trade, protection, and war. Religious institutions are permitted and respected, but they operate under state law. Kelemvor’s presence is especially visible through The Final Journey and its concern for proper death, lawful passage, funerary dignity, and the care of those who cannot afford grand rites. In Morfael, this work is practical rather than ceremonial. The dead still need washing whether or not anyone important knew their names. Selûne’s worship is quieter but deeply felt along the river. Travellers, sailors, night workers, widows, messengers, and people waiting for someone overdue are drawn to her lamps and water-shrines. Magic is common in the Crown, but regulated. It is taught, licensed, recorded, and directed toward useful service: medicine, architecture, investigation, mining, secure communication, military planning, education, and infrastructure. Unlicensed or unexplained magic draws attention quickly. Veinstone remains part of the Crown’s public history. Earlier Vermillion rulers used metals infused with veinstone from cliffs and riverbeds around the Godscar to create magical weaponry that helped establish the state’s military reputation. In the modern era, citizens are told the Crown’s strength rests less on any single material and more on control, wealth, schooling, military organisation, and command of movement. Culture and Status ¶ Vermillion culture is wealthy, educated, ambitious, and orderly. Status is shown through education, military rank, property, licensed trade rights, academy credentials, public service, and proximity to the Civic Directorate. The wealthy display success through white-stone houses, private tutors, riverfront properties, fine clothing, formal patronage, and access to restricted markets. Modest families work hard to place children in civic schools, trade academies, officer programmes, or state apprenticeships. The Crown does not present itself as cruel. Many citizens live comfortable lives and genuinely believe Maeron Cadris brought stability, safety, and national greatness. The danger of the Vermillion Crown lies in how much comfort depends on surveillance, controlled movement, military strength, and obedience. Morfael’s culture is less polished and more direct. People there value usefulness, memory, and practical loyalty. A person who can mend a chain, pole a ferry, calm a grieving widow, read a current, wash a body, or keep a secret has value. A person who only carries fine papers may still be left standing in the rain. Last updated: June 23, 2026

docs.text: Player-facing gazetteer for Caer Oryn, capital of the Vermillion Crown, and Morfael, the river town pressed against its outer edge. Caer Oryn is the polished face of Vermillion power: a white-stone capital of bridges, permits, academies, soldiers, civic schools, toll offices, formal temples, river chains, and watched streets. It is wealthy, educated, organised, and proud of being all three. Its citizens are taught that prosperity comes from discipline, and that discipline requires schooling, service, law, and loyalty to the state. Morfael is what sits below that order. It is close enough to the capital to be controlled by it, but far enough downriver and downhill to be ignored when convenient. It exists because Caer Oryn needs river labour, ferry crossings, customs records, cheap storage, fish markets, pauper burials, repair yards, and people willing to do work the upper city prefers not to see. This gazetteer is written for players. It contains public knowledge, visible institutions, common local texture, and places characters might reasonably know about or visit. It does not include hidden histories, DM-only explanations, encounter tables, stat blocks, or secret faction structures.

The town sits downstream of the city, where the River Oryn runs west toward Lake Tharne. Morfael grew where the capital did not want to look too closely. Morfael is not lawless, but it is not Caer Oryn either. It has watch posts, toll points, river chains, customs sheds, patrol routes, and Crown officers. It does not have the same clean order as the higher districts inside the capital. People come to Morfael when they need work, passage, cheap lodging, river access, or a place where the city’s rules are present but less polished. The town is crowded with boatmen, washerfolk, dock labourers, fishmongers, cart drivers, sewer workers, petty merchants, shrine-keepers, beggars, guards, pilgrims, and people who cannot afford to live properly inside Caer Oryn. Morfael should feel wet, lived-in, poor in places, useful to everyone, and trusted by no one. It is close to power, but rarely protected by it.
docs.title: Morfael: The Wet Edge of the Capital

docs.text: Broad stone steps where the river meets the town. Fisherfolk, laundresses, children, dockhands, ferrymen, paupers, and market runners use these steps every day. During flood season, the lower steps vanish under brown-green water. Locals treat the Flood Steps as ordinary, which is exactly why anything strange there becomes everyone’s business.
docs.title: The Flood Steps

docs.text: A cramped fish and salvage market near the Flood Steps. Its stalls sell river fish, smoked eel, cheap knives, netting, hooks, repaired boots, recovered river goods, broken tools, and cheap food. It is noisy, practical, and crowded enough that visitors can miss half of what matters.
docs.title: The Black Eel Market

docs.text: A small, practical chapel connected to The Final Journey . It serves drowned sailors, paupers, dock accidents, unidentified dead, grieving families, and those too poor to pay for formal rites in Caer Oryn. Its bell is old and cracked. Locals know its sound well.
docs.title: Chapel of the Last Lantern

docs.text: A small Selûnite alcove built into an old flood wall. A shallow basin holds river water. Sailors, ferrymen, widows, messengers, and travellers leave candles here before night crossings or long roads. It matters because ordinary people ask for safe passage here, write names of the missing, leave letters for those who may never return, and sit with uncertainty.
docs.title: Lumenwell Shrine

docs.text: A Crown-controlled customs and lock office near the canal mouth. It handles tolls, cargo seals, river permits, lock schedules, late fees, and arguments about missing stamps. Most Morfael residents dislike dealing with it, but nearly everyone depends on it working.
docs.title: The Red Lockhouse

docs.text: A chain ferry linking Morfael to the opposite bank and several river paths used by labourers, messengers, market folk, and people avoiding the longer official crossings. It is slow, noisy, useful, and part of the town’s daily rhythm.
docs.title: Harrowchain Ferry

docs.text: A low tavern near the quay. It serves fish stew, sour beer, dockside gossip, and cheap beds. It is not refined, but it is useful. In Morfael, that is often enough.
docs.title: The Hook and Bell

docs.text: A narrow records office where cargo manifests, letters, invoices, permits, dockside contracts, and discreet copies are written for people who cannot read or cannot easily deal with Caer Oryn’s formal offices.
docs.title: Vellum House

docs.text: A repair yard for carts, barges, cracked wheels, pulley frames, chain posts, hooks, dock hoists, and practical metalwork. If something breaks in Morfael and cannot be carried to Caer Oryn, it usually passes through Cairnwell Yard.
docs.title: Cairnwell Yard

docs.text: A narrow row of lodging houses, cheap rooms, widows’ rooms, and rented storage. It is cramped, damp, and never entirely quiet.
docs.title: Low Lantern Row

docs.text: The road climbing from Morfael toward the controlled outer approaches of Caer Oryn. City watch, Crown agents, tax carts, legal messengers, military clerks, and official processions use this road more than locals do.
docs.title: Marrowgate Road

docs.text: Cerys Varrow is the Crown-appointed reeve of Morfael. She manages taxes, dock complaints, street repairs, official notices, and the difficult work of answering to Caer Oryn while living among people who resent her authority. Watch-Corporal Dannel Strake is a lower-town watch corporal. He is tired, cautious, and not as corrupt as people assume. He wants order first and truth second, which makes him frustrating but not useless. Sister Halva Dorn is a dwarf lay-priest of the Chapel of the Last Lantern. She tends the poor dead, drowned sailors, unnamed bodies, and families who cannot afford the upper city. She is stern, compassionate, and difficult to intimidate. Eira Lorne keeps Lumenwell Shrine. She is not a grand priestess; she cleans the basin, lights candles, records names, comforts families, and remembers which riverfolk have not come home. Old Pell is the ferryman of Harrowchain Ferry. He knows the river better than the town watch knows its streets, speaks slowly, and notices everything. Mara Venn is a fishmonger at the Black Eel Market. She is loud, practical, and protective of local children. She knows who belongs in Morfael and who walks like they are pretending to belong. Joric Marn is a customs factor at the Red Lockhouse. He keeps records, stamps permits, and has mastered the official art of not understanding more than he is paid to understand. Elian Marr is a retired lock engineer. He knows old waterworks, service routes, and outdated mechanisms better than many current officials. Maelis Wren is an apothecary of Low Lantern Row. She sells poultices, sleep draughts, fever tinctures, dockhand liniment, and the kind of quiet help poor people seek before risking official attention.
docs.title: Public Faces of Morfael

docs.text: Caer Oryn’s law is written, recorded, witnessed, and procedural. A document can matter more than a sword if the seal is correct. A missing seal can make honest cargo look criminal. A bad ledger entry can stall a family business for months. Morfael’s law is rougher. The watch knows many offenders by name, but the town also knows when the watch chooses not to see something. Serious matters involving Crown officers, customs records, foreign travellers, military cargo, or suspicious river traffic can be pulled into Caer Oryn’s systems quickly. Once that happens, Morfael rarely hears the full story again. The Passage Directorate is the branch ordinary travellers most often fear. It controls permits, crossings, lock schedules, tolls, licensed river movement, and the practical right to pass from one place to another without being stopped. The public lesson is simple: movement through the Vermillion Crown is possible, profitable, and protected, but it is never truly free.
docs.title: Law, Order, and Daily Control

docs.text: Caer Oryn turns movement into power. Its wealth comes from river tolls, merchant charters, legal authority, civic schooling, military administration, academy training, public contracts, bridge control, lock control, customs enforcement, and the ability to make everyone else’s passage depend on Crown systems. Morfael survives on the physical work behind that wealth. Fish are smoked. Ropes are tarred. Ferries are poled. Carts are repaired. Bodies are washed. Letters are written. Cargo is shifted. Drains are cleared. Barges are patched. Names are remembered. The capital counts value in ledgers. Morfael counts it in favours, names, routes, and who will still open a door after dark.
docs.title: Economy and Trade

docs.text: The Vermillion Crown worships many gods, especially those associated with law, victory, wealth, civilisation, knowledge, craft, trade, protection, and war. Religious institutions are permitted and respected, but they operate under state law. Kelemvor’s presence is especially visible through The Final Journey and its concern for proper death, lawful passage, funerary dignity, and the care of those who cannot afford grand rites. In Morfael, this work is practical rather than ceremonial. The dead still need washing whether or not anyone important knew their names. Selûne’s worship is quieter but deeply felt along the river. Travellers, sailors, night workers, widows, messengers, and people waiting for someone overdue are drawn to her lamps and water-shrines. Magic is common in the Crown, but regulated. It is taught, licensed, recorded, and directed toward useful service: medicine, architecture, investigation, mining, secure communication, military planning, education, and infrastructure. Unlicensed or unexplained magic draws attention quickly. Veinstone remains part of the Crown’s public history. Earlier Vermillion rulers used metals infused with veinstone from cliffs and riverbeds around the Godscar to create magical weaponry that helped establish the state’s military reputation. In the modern era, citizens are told the Crown’s strength rests less on any single material and more on control, wealth, schooling, military organisation, and command of movement.
docs.title: Religion and Magic

docs.text: Vermillion culture is wealthy, educated, ambitious, and orderly. Status is shown through education, military rank, property, licensed trade rights, academy credentials, public service, and proximity to the Civic Directorate. The wealthy display success through white-stone houses, private tutors, riverfront properties, fine clothing, formal patronage, and access to restricted markets. Modest families work hard to place children in civic schools, trade academies, officer programmes, or state apprenticeships. The Crown does not present itself as cruel. Many citizens live comfortable lives and genuinely believe Maeron Cadris brought stability, safety, and national greatness. The danger of the Vermillion Crown lies in how much comfort depends on surveillance, controlled movement, military strength, and obedience. Morfael’s culture is less polished and more direct. People there value usefulness, memory, and practical loyalty. A person who can mend a chain, pole a ferry, calm a grieving widow, read a current, wash a body, or keep a secret has value. A person who only carries fine papers may still be left standing in the rain. Last updated: June 23, 2026
docs.title: Culture and Status

docs.text: The history of Lazuril is commonly divided into broad historical ages used by scholars, Scriptors, churches, archive houses, and historians. Exact dates remain heavily disputed. Different cultures use different historical systems, and some regions reject standardised chronology entirely. The major ages are therefore best understood as broad historical frameworks rather than universally agreed periods. Modern chronology throughout much of Arkhaven is measured from the beginning of The Green Silence , recognised as 1 GS. The current historical period is generally treated as 1200 GS , roughly 1,200 years after the Green Silence began. Age Before Memory ¶ The Age Before Memory refers to the earliest period of known history. Very little reliable information survives from this era. Most knowledge comes from: Fragmentary ruins Religious tradition Astronomical records Deep-earth discoveries Oral mythology Isolated archive fragments Several major civilisations are believed to have existed during this period, though little is known with certainty. Age of Fracture ¶ The Age of Fracture refers to the period surrounding The Godscar . The age is associated with: Continental upheaval Religious transformation Mass migration Political collapse Large-scale destruction Changes to geography and waterways The Godscar predates all currently documented peoples of Arkhaven. Modern cultures preserve interpretations and theories rather than direct knowledge of its true origin. Many churches treat this period as one of the defining moments in mortal history. Post-Godscar Era ¶ The Post-Godscar Era describes the long reconstruction period following the Age of Fracture. Several later kingdoms, churches, trade systems, and settlement patterns trace their origins to this period. The era also includes the establishment or expansion of several currently recognised peoples within Arkhaven. This includes early dwarven holds in the mountains, elven archive traditions in the south-western forests, and tabaxi communities in the northern rainforests. Much surviving written history begins during the later stages of this era. Era of Silence ¶ The Era of Silence begins with the Green Silence in 1 GS, roughly 1,200 years before the current era. The period is characterised by: Lost settlements Broken roads Disrupted records Isolated populations Disappearing forest regions Historical uncertainty Large gaps in surviving history originate from this era. The later human arrival known as the Arkfall occurred around 400 GS, roughly 800 years before the current era, after the Green Silence had begun and before the War of the False Saints. Arkborne histories record that a single Ark crossed the sea from Meritus , carrying 1,000 people: mostly humans, with some Aasimar lineages among them. Age of False Saints ¶ The Age of False Saints refers to the period surrounding War of the False Saints . The conflict is generally believed to have occurred around 700 GS, roughly 500 years before the current era. The age was marked by: Religious conflict Doctrinal instability False miracles Forged relics Saint cults Political manipulation of religion Human-led churches and states were major accelerants of the crisis, although they were not the only participants. The age eventually led to the creation of The Scriptor Compact , which was established around 750 GS, roughly 450 years before the current era. Compact Era ¶ The Compact Era is the current historical age used by many major institutions in Arkhaven. The era is characterised by: Increased record standardisation Greater institutional cooperation Expansion of archive systems Growth of trade networks Wider use of Scriptors Continued political fragmentation The current historical period is generally recognised as 1200 GS, roughly 1,200 years after the beginning of the Green Silence. Despite greater stability, many unresolved tensions from earlier ages remain active.

docs.text: The calendar systems of Lazuril vary between cultures, kingdoms, churches, and historical traditions. Most modern systems used in Arkhaven now measure time using the beginning of The Green Silence as the primary historical reference point. Under this system, the first recorded year of the Green Silence is recognised as 1 GS . The current historical period is generally treated as 1200 GS , roughly 1,200 years after the beginning of the event. Overview ¶ Most major calendars are based upon: Solar cycles Lunar observation Seasonal change Astronomical events Religious observance Although regional systems still exist, the GS dating system is widely used by: Churches Archive Houses Scriptors Trade institutions Historians Major governments Seasons ¶ Most regions recognise four major seasons. Seasonal intensity varies significantly depending on geography and climate. Northern rainforests, desert regions, mountain territories, and glacial elevations often experience seasonal conditions very differently from the central grasslands. Religious Observances ¶ Many churches maintain holy days, fasts, pilgrimage periods, and commemorative festivals tied to: Solstices Equinoxes Historical events Saints Celestial alignments Agricultural cycles Religious calendars do not always align between institutions. Astronomy and Navigation ¶ Astronomical observation remains important for: Navigation Agriculture Religious ritual Maritime travel Seasonal prediction Historical record keeping Elven observatories and maritime powers maintain some of the most accurate astronomical records. Historical Usage ¶ The adoption of the GS system became increasingly widespread after the War of the False Saints , which occurred roughly 500 years before the current era, and the expansion of institutional record keeping under The Scriptor Compact , established roughly 450 years before the current era. Many historians considered the Green Silence a more stable historical reference point than earlier disputed events associated with the Godscar. Older records may therefore use different chronological systems. Current Status ¶ Although no single calendar system dominates all of Lazuril, the GS dating system is now the closest equivalent to a continental standard throughout much of Arkhaven. Regional variations remain common, especially in isolated territories and older religious traditions.

docs.text: Academy Quarter: NPCs & Locations ¶ Player-facing reference for NPCs met and locations visited in the Academy Quarter of Caer Oryn. Updated after Session 4 - The Hart of the Matter. NPCs Met ¶ NPC First Encountered What the Party Knows Quincy Adams Inkglass Apothecary An apothecary and healer who already had a warm working relationship with Teclis. He identified the red dust recovered from Edrin Vaal as veinstone, agreed to examine the sample and supplied the party with two heavily discounted healing potions. Elowen Inkglass Apothecary Quincy's assistant. She treated Nakoa's injuries in the back room despite never having provided first aid to a tabaxi before. Mentioned, Not Met ¶ No additional named NPCs were mentioned during the party's recorded visit to the Academy Quarter. Locations Visited ¶ Location What Happened There Inkglass Apothecary The party brought Nakoa here for treatment and showed Quincy Adams the red dust recovered from Edrin Vaal. Quincy identified it as veinstone from the Crimson Chain, explained some of its former uses in weapons and magical implements and agreed to study the sample further. Known Open Threads ¶ Quincy needs more veinstone material before he can conduct a fuller examination. The party intended to return after giving Quincy several days to inspect the sample. Red veinstone is the most common known variety, implying that other colours and properties may exist. Veinstone mining has largely ceased, while much of the remaining material is believed to be held by noble houses and the Crown. The precise way veinstone was used on Edrin Vaal, and whether it caused his reanimation and violent surges, remains unknown.

docs.text: Foundry Quarter: NPCs & Locations ¶ Player-facing reference for NPCs met and locations visited in the Foundry Quarter of Caer Oryn. Updated after Session 4 - The Hart of the Matter. NPCs Met ¶ NPC First Encountered What the Party Knows Foundry Quarter Gate Guards Quarter entrance Two guards refused to accept Teclis' Inquisitor-Scriptor authority without the correct papers from Arch-Lector Voss. Teclis distracted them with an illusion involving one guard's wife and the other's supposed betrayal, allowing the party to slip into the restricted quarter. Local Foundry Worker 17 Magpie Lane Confirmed that number 17 had once been a shift manager's office but had stood unused for months. Magpie Lane Blacksmith Magpie Lane Saw Halwin enter 17 Magpie Lane before several cloaked figures followed. He heard a scuffle and said anyone leaving without passing his forge must have used the sewer drain or the scaffolding at the closed end of the lane. Garron Duskholt Rooftops above Magpie Lane A human agent of the Obsidian Register who shot Cassian and was captured after a rooftop chase. He carried the crying-eye brand on the back of his neck. Under interrogation, he revealed the Gilded Hart room 13 drop, Odran Kesh's name and the use of the Magpie Lane drain as a transport route. He was killed in the basement beneath number 17. Mentioned, Not Met ¶ NPC Connection Halwin Seen entering 17 Magpie Lane shortly before several cloaked figures. His role in the struggle and disappearance from the building remains unknown. Odran Kesh Named by Garron Duskholt as his superior within the Obsidian Register. Garron said Kesh could be found at the Counting House in the Foundry Quarter. Locations Visited ¶ Location What Happened There Foundry Quarter Entrance The quarter was under tighter control during preparations for Cadris' Day. The party were refused entry without formal papers and slipped through while the guards were distracted by Teclis' illusion. Magpie Lane A smoke-stained working lane containing number 17, a nearby blacksmith's forge and a closed cul-de-sac at its far end. The party followed Edrin Vaal's courier route here, questioned local workers and discovered possible escape routes through a large sewer drain and rooftop scaffolding. 17 Magpie Lane A derelict former shift manager's office. The front room was dusty, while the rear showed signs of a struggle, including broken furniture and a concealed doorway disguised by an illusion of brick mortar. The party later brought Garron Duskholt back here for interrogation. Hidden Basement beneath 17 Magpie Lane Contained barrels of old vegetables, a trapped gilded chest, Veylrain cloth and a courier tag linking Edrin Vaal to a small green lizard figure. Blood seeped between the floorboards and dragged marks suggested an injured person had been moved through the room. Garron Duskholt was interrogated and killed here. Scaffolding and Rooftops The party investigated the lane's upper escape route after Cassian was struck by a crossbow bolt. Nakoa pursued the attacker across the rooftops, aided by Teclis and Alekthar, until Garron fell into a barrel below and was captured. Known Open Threads ¶ Odran Kesh was said to be based at the Counting House and has not yet been confronted. Halwin's fate and his connection to the cloaked figures remain unknown. Edrin Vaal was taken through the Magpie Lane drain, but the destination beyond the drain remains unknown. Blood and drag marks beneath number 17 suggest another injured captive or victim was moved through the basement. The small green lizard figure was not recovered at Magpie Lane and was also gone when room 13 of the Gilded Hart was later searched. The Obsidian Register's wider structure, purpose and operations within the Foundry Quarter remain unresolved.

Under interrogation, he revealed the Gilded Hart room 13 drop, Odran Kesh's name and the use of the Magpie Lane drain as a transport route. He was killed in the basement beneath number 17.

docs.text: Location What Happened There Foundry Quarter Entrance The quarter was under tighter control during preparations for Cadris' Day. The party were refused entry without formal papers and slipped through while the guards were distracted by Teclis' illusion. Magpie Lane A smoke-stained working lane containing number 17, a nearby blacksmith's forge and a closed cul-de-sac at its far end. The party followed Edrin Vaal's courier route here, questioned local workers and discovered possible escape routes through a large sewer drain and rooftop scaffolding. 17 Magpie Lane A derelict former shift manager's office. The front room was dusty, while the rear showed signs of a struggle, including broken furniture and a concealed doorway disguised by an illusion of brick mortar. The party later brought Garron Duskholt back here for interrogation. Hidden Basement beneath 17 Magpie Lane Contained barrels of old vegetables, a trapped gilded chest, Veylrain cloth and a courier tag linking Edrin Vaal to a small green lizard figure. Blood seeped between the floorboards and dragged marks suggested an injured person had been moved through the room. Garron Duskholt was interrogated and killed here. Scaffolding and Rooftops The party investigated the lane's upper escape route after Cassian was struck by a crossbow bolt. Nakoa pursued the attacker across the rooftops, aided by Teclis and Alekthar, until Garron fell into a barrel below and was captured.

NPCs Met ¶ NPC First Encountered What the Party Knows Sister Halva Dorn Chapel of the Last Lantern A practical lay-priest connected to The Final Journey. She gathered the party over missing people, suspicious cargo records, red stone dust and rumours of bodies washing up in the river. When the party returned from Caer Oryn, she passed on that Dannel Strake was looking for them, received their warnings about robed figures and was asked to help mark suspicious Amakiir-labelled shipments through Old Pell. Lysa Black Eel Market A Morfael local who spoke with Cassian and Nakoa. She had seen a military-style bandage marked with a small stamp, but let it wash further downriver before realising its significance. Lerris Black Eel Market A market local who sat with Lysa and spoke with Cassian and Nakoa. He offered food while the group gathered information. Tovin Rusk Black Eel Market A young witness. He told Alekthar and Teclis about an earlier figure rising from the river with gold shining beneath the skin. He later spotted another shape in the water. Watch-Corporal Dannel Strake Flood Steps A lower-town watch corporal. He arrived after the fight, gave the party a short window before reporting upward and directed them to Edrin Vaal's room at Gullhook Loft. He said this was not the first reanimation report. By the party's return to Morfael, he was seeking guidance on what to report about Edrin's death and the party's involvement. Edrin Vaal Flood Steps The missing courier. His body washed up from the River Oryn marked with red dust, puncture wounds, medical bandages and the brand S-V-AUG-03 . He reanimated in panic, triggered a violent surge and was destroyed at the river's edge. Mentioned, Not Met ¶ NPC Connection Rennic Sallow Mentioned as the middle-man through whom Nakoa received word that a courier had gone missing and that the matter was worth his attention. Arch-Lector Meren Voss Mentioned as the superior who sent Teclis from The Final Journey to investigate rumours of undeath in Morfael. Eira Lorne Helped gather the list of missing people that Sister Halva Dorn gave to Cassian. Old Pell Operator of the Harrowchain Ferry. The party asked Sister Dorn whether he could place recognisable offering-box items into shipments whose manifests bore the Amakiir sigil. Locations Visited ¶ Location What Happened There Chapel of the Last Lantern The party first gathered here at Sister Halva Dorn's request. The meeting concerned missing people, river rumours, suspicious cargo and questionable manifests. Halva also gave Cassian a list of missing names gathered with Eira Lorne's help. After returning from Caer Oryn, the party reported their findings, warned that Morfael needed stronger night patrols and discussed using chapel offerings to mark suspicious Amakiir-labelled shipments. Black Eel Market A wet, busy riverside market near the Flood Steps. The party split their enquiries here: Cassian and Nakoa spoke with Lysa and Lerris, while Alekthar and Teclis spoke with Tovin. The market was full of traders, eel tubs, smoke, gulls, food, mud and river traffic. Flood Steps The stone steps below the Black Eel Market where Edrin Vaal's body washed ashore. The party identified him as the missing courier, discovered his brand and red dust, witnessed his reanimation and fought him at the river's edge. Gullhook Loft A cramped room above the street where Edrin Vaal had been staying. Nakoa opened the locked door with Alekthar's guidance. Inside, the party found courier tags, wax scraps, a writing board and signs that Edrin's most recent route pointed toward Magpie Lane in the Foundry Quarter of Caer Oryn. A hidden floor panel concealed Veylrain cloth, a red candle with faint gold shimmer and a small wooden idol shaped like a stamp. The base of the stamp was carved to match the sigil of House Amakiir. Known Open Threads ¶ Edrin Vaal was branded S-V-AUG-03 . The red dust found around Edrin's teeth, nails and wounds was later identified as veinstone. Strake said Edrin was the third reported reanimation and still needs to decide what he will report upward. The party warned that robed figures may still be using Morfael's streets and riverside routes, particularly after dark. The hidden bundle at Gullhook Loft linked Veylrain cloth, red-gold wax, courier work and the stolen shape of House Amakiir authority. Sister Dorn was asked to help establish a recognisable marker for suspicious shipments bearing the Amakiir sigil.

docs.text: Aarakocra ¶ Aarakocra are avian people found mainly in the northern jungles, high canopy regions, cliffs, ridgelines, and storm-watched mountains of Arkhaven . Northern Skies ¶ Aarakocra live among the northern clanlands, including the Veylrath Clans , Jhakur Clans , Zul’Akari Clans , and parts of The Skeldic Concord . Some are also found in the Kharad Wildlands , where cliffs and open winds suit them well. Their settlements are usually built in high trees, cliff ledges, stone needles, ruined towers, or mountain shelves that are difficult for ground-bound enemies to reach. They often act as scouts, messengers, weather-watchers, hunters, and guardians of high places. Freedom and Watchfulness ¶ Aarakocra culture values freedom, wind, height, clear sight, family roosts, and warning calls. Many communities are wary of enclosed cities and lowland politics, but they understand the value of trade with those who respect their sky-routes. To other peoples, aarakocra are often mysterious, distant, and difficult to hold to earthly borders. In northern Arkhaven, however, their ability to watch movement from above makes them essential allies, dangerous enemies, and some of the best messengers in the continent’s wild regions.

docs.text: Aasimar ¶ Aasimar are rare human-descended bloodlines on Arkhaven , marked by traces of celestial ancestry carried across the sea aboard the Ark. Arkborne Nobility ¶ They did not arrive as a separate people or wandering outsiders. The first Aasimar families came among the 1,000 passengers of the Ark, alongside early human nobility, priests, officers, and chosen settlers who helped establish the first human foothold on the continent. The arrival, later remembered as the Arkfall, occurred around 400 GS, roughly 800 years before the current era. Because of their status, many Aasimar bloodlines were granted large plots of land in the new world. For generations, these families benefited from early claims, inherited estates, temple patronage, civic office, and the prestige of being linked to the Ark’s founding families. Modern Bloodlines ¶ In modern Arkhaven, Aasimar are most strongly associated with old human states such as the Republic of Havenor , where several respected families still claim celestial ancestry from the first arrivals. Their bloodlines are often treated with reverence, suspicion, or resentment depending on local history. Not all Aasimar are wealthy or noble today. Some families lost their lands, diluted their claims, or rejected the privileges of their ancestors. Even so, the old association remains: to many people of Arkhaven, Aasimar are living reminders of the Ark, the first human settlement, and the unequal rewards that followed.

docs.text: Dwarves ¶ Dwarves are one of the major civilised peoples of Arkhaven . They are most strongly associated with the south-eastern mountain ranges of the continent, where their oldest kingdoms, deepest mines, and largest strongholds are located. Mountain Realms ¶ Their principal homeland is The Throne of Khuldovar , centred on the great mountain-capital of Khuldovar. The Dornhal Empire is also dwarven, though culturally and politically distinct, having split from Khuldovar many centuries ago. Large dwarven holds, mining enclaves, fortress-cities, tunnel stations, and trade halls exist throughout the mountain regions of Arkhaven. Smaller dwarven communities are also found near human cities, major construction projects, river routes, strategic passes, and mixed states such as the Windmere Assembly . Stone, Craft and Memory ¶ Dwarven civilisation is shaped by stone, metal, pressure, heat, and depth. Their settlements are commonly built within mountains rather than upon them, and many dwarven societies measure wealth, prestige, and history through craftsmanship, engineering, oath-keeping, and the endurance of their halls. Dwarves are widely respected as miners, masons, smiths, armourers, engineers, bridge-builders, and fortification experts. Human and mixed states often rely on dwarven skill for roads, walls, tunnels, weapons, locks, and stonework. Their societies are usually organised around clans, guilds, ancestral lineages, and sworn obligations. Political disputes between dwarven powers can be severe, but dwarven contracts are generally treated across Arkhaven as among the most reliable in the world. In modern Arkhaven, dwarves remain economically powerful beyond their population size. Their mountains provide metal, stone, engineering knowledge, military strength, and deep historical memory. To many dwarves, the deep earth is not only a source of wealth. It is history itself.

docs.text: Elves ¶ Elves are one of the oldest surviving peoples of Arkhaven . Their civilisation predates most modern kingdoms, organised churches, and written human histories on the continent. The Silent Weald ¶ They are most strongly associated with the south-western forests, especially the region now known as the Silent Weald after The Green Silence . Most major elven settlements, archives, academies, noble houses, and sacred groves remain concentrated in these forests. The main elven powers include The Martarië Crown , Tirith I Daur , Houses of Bârathanaear , The Eldermarch Court , and the Court of Thalóriel . Elves also hold influence in mixed states such as the Verdant Confederacy and the Windmere Assembly . Memory and Influence ¶ Elven society places unusually high importance on continuity, memory, language, education, magical discipline, and the preservation of knowledge. This became even more important after the Green Silence, when large parts of older elven culture were swallowed by the forest and many records were lost. Because of this history, elves are diligent record keepers. Documents are copied, witnessed, translated, sealed, and stored in separate archives so that history cannot vanish in the same way again. This cultural habit is one of the main reasons elves became closely involved in the creation and operation of The Scriptor Compact . Elven magic is usually associated with illusion, divination, enchantment, warding, preservation, ritual practice, and memory. After the War of the False Saints , elven illusionists became controversial, but also valuable, because they were among the best suited to identifying false miracles and magical deception. In modern Arkhaven, elves remain one of the continent’s major political, scholarly, and religious influences. Their population is smaller than humanity’s, but their long lives, archives, magical education, and Scriptor institutions allow them to hold influence far beyond their numbers.

docs.text: Firbolgs ¶ Firbolgs are quiet, powerful forest and wildland people found in scattered communities across Arkhaven . They are most often associated with deep woods, old groves, mountain forests, hidden valleys, and places where the boundary between settlement and wilderness remains thin. Hidden Stewards ¶ Firbolgs are known in the Kharad Wildlands , the northern rainforest clans, and the older forest edges of elven territory. Some live among the Veylrath Clans , while others keep to remote groves, abandoned shrines, high meadows, and concealed communities that rarely appear on maps. Their culture values patience, restraint, hospitality, spiritual duty, and the protection of natural places. Many firbolgs avoid cities not because they fear civilisation, but because they see settled peoples as loud, hurried, wasteful, and dangerous when left unwatched. Reputation and Role ¶ Firbolgs are often treated as gentle giants by outsiders, though this reputation is only partly true. They prefer peace, but they are not harmless. A firbolg community can be terrifying when defending a sacred grove, hidden spring, burial mound, or forest boundary. In modern Arkhaven, firbolgs are usually encountered as druids, shamans, wardens, healers, hermits, guides, or quiet members of frontier communities. They rarely seek power, but they often remember old boundaries better than the rulers who claim to own the land.

docs.text: Genasi ¶ Genasi are rare people whose bloodlines carry the influence of elemental power. They may be born among many peoples of Arkhaven , though their presence is most often linked to places where the world feels unstable, charged, or unusually close to raw elemental forces. Elemental Bloodlines ¶ Most scholars divide genasi into air, earth, fire, and water lineages, though local traditions use many different names. Air genasi are associated with high mountains, stormlands, exposed cliffs, and impossible winds. Earth genasi are tied to deep stone, caverns, fault lines, mines, and ancient buried places. Fire genasi are linked to forge districts, volcanic heat, magical fire, desert rites, and old pacts with flame. Water genasi are most often found near rivers, lakes, coasts, floods, and scarred waterways. In Arkhaven, many people connect genasi to the lingering powers of The Godscar , the deep mountain realms of the Dwarves , the flood-prone lands of The Skeldic Concord , and the river cultures of the north. Place in Arkhaven ¶ Genasi are too rare to form a single state or unified culture. Most are raised among the people into which they are born, though their elemental nature often marks them as unusual, blessed, cursed, or dangerous. Some become sailors, smiths, shamans, storm-watchers, ruin-delvers, healers, guards, mages, or wandering specialists. Their reputation depends heavily on the element they carry and the culture judging them. A water genasi may be honoured in a floodland village, while a fire genasi may be feared in a town that still remembers holy wars and burning shrines.

docs.text: Gnomes ¶ Gnomes are a small, clever, and widely scattered people of Arkhaven . Like Halflings , they existed on the continent before the arrival of Humans , though most gnomish communities were too dispersed or hidden to form large states of their own. Hidden Settlements ¶ Gnomes are found across the continent in workshops, burrows, river towns, university districts, forest enclaves, and trade cities. Forest gnomes are especially important in the Myruun Clans , where their hidden paths, trapcraft, herbalism, illusion magic, concealed shelters, and small-scale invention help protect clan settlements. Other gnomish communities live in the Windmere Assembly , dwarven mountain towns, human cities, and isolated woodland settlements. They are rarely politically dominant, but their technical and magical skill makes them difficult to ignore. Craft and Curiosity ¶ Gnomish culture is shaped by curiosity, invention, careful observation, humour, and the protection of hidden places. Many gnomes favour illusion, clockwork, alchemy, mapping, trapmaking, banking, scholarship, or magical craft. In modern Arkhaven, gnomes are usually seen as useful, strange, secretive, and brilliant in equal measure. Their small settlements often survive by being hard to find, harder to understand, and too valuable for neighbouring powers to casually threaten.

docs.text: Gnomish culture is shaped by curiosity, invention, careful observation, humour, and the protection of hidden places. Many gnomes favour illusion, clockwork, alchemy, mapping, trapmaking, banking, scholarship, or magical craft. In modern Arkhaven, gnomes are usually seen as useful, strange, secretive, and brilliant in equal measure. Their small settlements often survive by being hard to find, harder to understand, and too valuable for neighbouring powers to casually threaten.
docs.title: Craft and Curiosity

docs.text: Goblins ¶ Goblins are small, quick, and stubbornly adaptable people found across the rougher margins of Arkhaven , especially in jungles, ruins, tunnels, marshes, frontier towns, and places larger powers do not fully control. Clan and Warren Peoples ¶ Batiri goblins are one of the recognised peoples of the Zul’Akari Clans , where they live among the jungle, marsh, lake, and ruin territories of the north-west. Other goblin groups exist in caves, old fortifications, abandoned mines, city underworks, battlefield ruins, and hidden camps across the continent. Goblins rarely hold formal power in large states, but they are difficult to remove once established. Their communities survive through numbers, cunning, salvage, traps, scavenging, bargaining, and a willingness to make homes in places others consider worthless or cursed. Reputation and Survival ¶ Most larger peoples view goblins with suspicion, often reducing them to pests, thieves, raiders, or servants of stronger monsters. This reputation is not always fair, but goblin bands are practical enough to use fear and confusion when it keeps them alive. In modern Arkhaven, goblins may be enemies, guides, miners, smugglers, tinkers, scouts, relic-looters, labourers, or uneasy members of mixed frontier communities. Their greatest strength is not power. It is refusal to disappear.

docs.text: Goliaths ¶ Goliaths are a large, powerful people most strongly associated with the harsh highlands, dry plains, and mountain edges of the Kharad Wildlands and the wider Thornbelt. Wildland Tribes ¶ Goliath communities are tribal, mobile, spiritual, and honour-bound. They live in mountain camps, highland routes, dry river valleys, cliff shelters, and seasonal gathering grounds where survival depends on endurance, strength, memory, and respect for the land. They are common in the colder southern mountains of the Kharad Wildlands, though many roam down into the plains. Some goliath bands trade with Loxodon tribes, dwarven prospectors, or nomadic human and halfling groups, but they rarely accept foreign rule easily. Honour and Spirit ¶ Goliath culture values personal honour, physical trial, ancestral memory, spiritual signs, oathkeeping, and proven usefulness. Boasting is common, but empty boasting is despised. A person’s worth is measured by what they endure, what they protect, and whether they carry their obligations without complaint. To settled peoples, goliaths are often seen as wildings, raiders, guides, mountain warriors, or spiritual nomads. To themselves, they are keepers of hard places, bound to winds, stone, beasts, ancestors, and the old laws of survival.

docs.text: Half-Orcs ¶ Half-orcs are people of mixed orcish and human ancestry, most commonly found in the frontier regions where Humans and Orcs have lived, fought, traded, raided, married, and survived alongside one another for generations. Frontier Bloodlines ¶ Half-orcs are especially common around the Kharad Wildlands , The Skeldic Concord , border towns, caravan roads, military settlements, and rough human frontier states. Their families may come from unions of love, alliance, captivity, adoption, survival, or simple proximity in hard lands where bloodline matters less than whether someone can be trusted. They are not a single culture. Some are raised in orcish clan traditions, some in human towns, some in Skeldic oath-bands, and some between both worlds without being fully accepted by either. Reputation and Place ¶ Half-orcs are often valued for strength, endurance, courage, and practicality, but they also face suspicion from people who reduce them to old stories of raiding and border violence. In modern Arkhaven, many half-orcs become soldiers, labourers, guards, hunters, smiths, scouts, oath-speakers, mercenaries, or adventurers. The most respected among them are those who turn divided ancestry into social advantage, able to move between cultures that would otherwise refuse to speak.

docs.text: Halflings ¶ Halflings are a small, adaptable people spread across Arkhaven . They existed on the continent before the arrival of Humans , though they were rarely organised into large kingdoms of their own. Scattered Communities ¶ Halflings are found throughout farming villages, river settlements, orchard towns, caravan routes, trade ports, and mixed states such as the Windmere Assembly . Small nomadic or dryland halfling groups are also known in the Kharad Wildlands . Their communities tend to be local, practical, and family-centred rather than imperial. Many survived human expansion by adapting quickly, joining new towns, negotiating land rights, or becoming indispensable as farmers, cooks, traders, scribes, guides, and mediators. Reputation and Culture ¶ Halflings are often underestimated by larger peoples, which has helped them survive. They are widely regarded as sociable, stubborn, lucky, observant, and difficult to fully uproot once they have made a place home. In modern Arkhaven, halflings rarely dominate politics, but they are present almost everywhere. Their influence is quiet, domestic, commercial, and agricultural, built through kinship networks, market trust, hospitality, and deep knowledge of local land.

docs.text: Humans ¶ Humans are the most widespread and politically dominant people on Arkhaven , but they are not considered native to the continent. The Arkborne ¶ Human histories describe their arrival by sea aboard a single colossal vessel, the Ark. The Ark carried 1,000 people west from Meritus : mostly humans, including sailors, settlers, priests, soldiers, craftspeople, scholars, officers, nobles, and families, with a smaller number of Aasimar lineages among them. The arrival, later remembered as the Arkfall, occurred around 400 GS, roughly 800 years before the current era, after the Green Silence had begun and before the War of the False Saints. The name Arkhaven is human in origin: to the earliest settlers, the continent was a haven reached by ark. The first Arkborne landing is most strongly associated with the Republic of Havenor , the oldest human-founded state on the continent. From these early coastal settlements, humans expanded inland over generations, founding farms, towns, churches, roads, ports, and fortified states. Human States ¶ Today, humans dominate or strongly influence several major realms, including the Republic of Havenor, The Vermillion Crown , the Verdant Confederacy , and the Windmere Assembly . Human populations also exist in many mixed regions, frontier settlements, trade towns, religious centres, and conquered or contested territories. Human power in Arkhaven is based on adaptation, population growth, agriculture, settlement expansion, trade, religious organisation, military flexibility, and political ambition. There is no single human ruler. Human states compete with one another as often as they compete with neighbouring peoples. Legacy ¶ The human legacy is contested. Many humans see themselves as descendants of desperate survivors who crossed the sea and built a new home. Older peoples often remember the same process as colonisation, land seizure, displacement, treaty-breaking, forced conversion, and cultural absorption. Human-led churches and states were major accelerants of the War of the False Saints , which occurred around 700 GS, roughly 500 years before the current era. Their institutions were younger, their records less stable, and their rulers were eager for divine legitimacy. This history contributed directly to the later authority of The Scriptor Compact , established around 750 GS, roughly 450 years before the current era. In modern Arkhaven, humans control many of the continent’s largest cities, farmland regions, trade routes, ports, churches, and armies. Their central legacy remains one of survival becoming entitlement.

docs.text: Kenku ¶ Kenku are a sharp-eyed, quick-handed people found in cities, ports, clan territories, caravan camps, and northern jungle settlements across Arkhaven . Mimics and Messengers ¶ Kenku are known for mimicry, memory, scavenging, trade talk, coded speech, and survival in crowded or dangerous places. In the northern regions they appear among the Veylrath Clans , Myruun Clans , and Zul’Akari Clans . They are also common enough in frontier settlements, dock districts, and travelling camps to be recognised across much of the continent. Many kenku serve as messengers, scouts, lookouts, translators, thieves, performers, spies, shrine attendants, market runners, and record-keepers of spoken things. Their ability to repeat voices, warnings, passwords, bird calls, and overheard conversations gives them a reputation that is both useful and unsettling. Reputation and Survival ¶ Kenku communities are usually small, practical, and socially flexible. They often live under the protection of stronger groups, but this does not make them weak. Kenku survive by knowing what others forget, hearing what others miss, and leaving before trouble closes around them. In modern Arkhaven, they are treated with mixed suspicion and respect. A kenku can be dismissed as a street mimic or valued as the only witness who remembers exactly what was said.

docs.text: Kobolds ¶ Kobolds are small reptilian people found in mines, caves, jungle ruins, marsh settlements, old tunnels, and scar-adjacent places across Arkhaven . Tunnels and Ruins ¶ Kobolds are one of the scaled peoples of the Jhakur Clans , where they live among rainforest, swamp, lake shore, and vine-choked ruin systems. Other kobold groups are found beneath human towns, near dwarven mines, around abandoned fortresses, and in tunnels too small or unstable for larger peoples to claim comfortably. Many kobold communities organise around warrens, brood houses, trap networks, shrine chambers, mining claims, or old draconic stories. Some venerate dragons, dragonborn ancestors, buried monsters, or whatever ancient power their warren believes protects it. Cunning and Survival ¶ Kobolds are often dismissed as weak by larger peoples, but that judgement gets many intruders killed. Kobolds survive through numbers, traps, narrow passages, warning systems, ambush routes, scavenged engineering, and obsessive knowledge of their home ground. In modern Arkhaven, kobolds may be miners, tunnel scouts, trappers, smugglers, ruin-diggers, sewer workers, monster-handlers, or clan auxiliaries. They are rarely respected in open society, but every wise commander knows better than to chase kobolds into tunnels they prepared themselves.

docs.text: Lizardfolk ¶ Lizardfolk are reptilian people found mainly in the northern jungles, marshes, wetlands, river deltas, lake shores, and flooded forests of Arkhaven . Northern Jungles ¶ Lizardfolk are important among the Jhakur Clans , where they form part of the scaled, shelled, venomous, and marsh-born peoples who dominate the northern jungle frontier. They also appear within the Zul’Akari Clans , Veylrath Clans , and Myruun Clans , though their role varies by region. Their settlements are usually built around rivers, reed beds, mud islands, tree roots, submerged platforms, cave mouths, warm stones, and sacred pools. Many communities are difficult for outsiders to identify, especially during flood seasons. Territory and Memory ¶ Lizardfolk culture is practical, territorial, and deeply tied to hunting rights, nesting grounds, river crossings, old ruins, and ancestral waters. They are not naturally cruel, but they often think in terms of survival, usefulness, threat, and obligation rather than human ideas of politeness or sentiment. In modern Arkhaven, lizardfolk are often feared by frontier settlers because of old conflicts over northern land. To the lizardfolk, those same conflicts are remembered as defence against intrusion into lands that were already hunted, guarded, and inhabited long before human roads reached the jungle edge.

docs.text: Orcs ¶ Orcs are a hardy people originally associated with the arid plains, scrublands, and flood-prone frontiers of northern Arkhaven , especially the Thornbelt and Floodlands. Thornbelt and Floodlands ¶ Older orcish communities lived as roaming clans, raiders, herders, hunters, and warrior bands across the harsh country now linked to the Kharad Wildlands and The Skeldic Concord . Their cultures were tribal at heart, built around strength, oath, kinship, survival, and the ability to move with the land rather than dominate it permanently. As human states expanded and frontier societies hardened, many orcs were pushed into service, exile, mercenary work, or mixed settlements. Others adapted into Skeldic oath-bands, Kharad trade gatherings, frontier militias, and city labour forces. Adaptation and Decline ¶ Orc culture has survived, but time has not treated it gently. Old clan laws, oral histories, war-songs, and sacred migration routes have been fragmented by settlement pressure, mixed ancestry, military recruitment, and poverty. Modern orcs can be found across Arkhaven as soldiers, caravan guards, smiths, labourers, hunters, mercenaries, farmers, and clan elders trying to preserve what remains. Many are still tribesmen at heart, even when living in cities that no longer understand the culture they came from.

docs.text: Tabaxi ¶ Tabaxi are a feline humanoid people found primarily in the northern territories of Arkhaven , especially within the tropical rainforests, dense jungle, river basins, and coastal forest regions. Northern Clanlands ¶ They are most strongly associated with the clan-held lands of the north, including the Veylrath Clans , Jhakur Clans , Myruun Clans , and Zul’Akari Clans . These regions are not ruled as single centralised kingdoms, and many tabaxi communities remain organised around kin-groups, treetop settlements, river clans, shrine families, and travelling bands. Tabaxi culture is shaped by movement, curiosity, oral tradition, sign language, hunting, trade secrecy, and survival in difficult forest terrain. Many settlements are built high in the canopy, with hidden platforms, rope bridges, rain collectors, lookout perches, and concealed nursery spaces. Reputation and Survival ¶ Outsiders often know tabaxi as agile scouts, guides, traders, messengers, and storytellers. Their knowledge of northern forest routes is valuable, but rarely given away freely. A tabaxi guide may lead travellers through the jungle, but most will never reveal the full location of a clan home or canopy road. Tabaxi communities are cautious because they have a long history of defending themselves from predators, raiders, traffickers, and those who attempted to capture young tabaxi for sale. This has made secrecy a cultural necessity rather than simple suspicion. Some tabaxi live in port towns, trade cities, or mixed frontier settlements, but most remain culturally tied to the hidden communities of the northern forests. Their central concern is survival without captivity, trade without exposure, and freedom without surrendering the safety of their young.

docs.text: Tieflings ¶ Tieflings are a scattered people found throughout Arkhaven , marked by infernal or fiendish traits that set them apart from the communities into which they are born. Rumours of Origin ¶ No single explanation for tieflings is accepted. Some people believe tieflings are born from families touched by the Godscar , especially those who drank too deeply from scar-tainted waters or lived too close to red lakes and old veinstone deposits. Others claim tieflings are blood creations of the Nine Hells, the result of bargains made by parents, ancestors, priests, nobles, or desperate families whose deals passed consequences down through the bloodline. Place in Arkhaven ¶ Tieflings can appear in almost any state, race, or class, which makes them difficult for churches and rulers to categorise. Some live openly in cities and ports, while others hide their features or leave hostile settlements before suspicion becomes violence. They are often looked down upon, feared, or treated as walking evidence of sin, corruption, or bad blood. Wealth, office, magical power, military service, or noble patronage can protect a tiefling from open abuse, but only if they are strong enough or useful enough to make others think twice.
